Massey's surface brightness test. With the aid of RCSDC and these visualization tools,
we can also explore and correlate large sets of quasar and galaxy spectra, discovering
patterns and trends that would be time-consuming to investigate individually. The
visualization tools are readily accessible online via web interfaces or as downloadable
versions for local use, with the source code freely available on GitHub.

The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing the pre-rift basin geometry from various models and well data revealed a distinct difference in the basin's shape, with the South Tropic Zone exhibiting an anomalously narrow section.  Our research indicates that this feature can be explained by the Early Jurassic opening of the Central Atlantic and is supported by heat flow anomalies, magmatism, and paleomagnetism data, all of which suggest a connection to the South Atlantic's formation.

A proven strategy to enhance multiple tasks using limited labeled data is
unsupervised pre-training.  Despite being a viable approach, contrastive
learning poses challenges in forming relevant pairs for an unsupervised
segmentation task like optical flow.  To overcome these challenges, we propose
using a set of simple, easily implemented tasks to generate positive and
negative pairs that are both massively scalable and near-optimal.  Our proposed
method, Contrastive Pre-training for Optical Flow, achieves the best results so
far on the KITTI and Sintel datasets, demonstrating significant improvements
over the current state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised optical flow
methods.  Moreover, our proposed method yields the most robust physical world
generalization among all unsupervised optical flow approaches.

We present how we overcame a major obstacle for NLP researchers by creating nearly 300 hours of audio transcripts from a Dungeons and Dragons game called D&D Live. These transcripts depict a text-based adventure where a Dungeon Master narrates events in response to a player's typed commands. Our recorded episode, set in the world of Greyhawk, features an engaged 20-year-old player navigating through various challenges. We provide easily accessible access to our dataset through the Storytelling200 website, which also offers supplementary materials such as visual aids, texts, audio, and insights into our data collection process. Additionally, we highlight how our dataset can advance the development of text-based multimodal agents by presenting the complex role of the Dungeon Master.

Despite significant research on Lexical Semantic Change Detection, most approaches remain limited to standard model assessments. This study deviates from this focus, shifting towards change discovery - identifying previously unknown word meanings emerging over time within a comprehensive corpus vocabulary. By extensively fine-tuning both a type-based and a token-based methodology on German datasets, our work showcases their applicability in discovering new words with evolving meanings. Additionally, our proposed methodology may contribute to several fields, including historical linguistics, language pathology, and the development of robust NLP systems.

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes remains an area of ongoing investigation. Recent studies have highlighted the importance of analyzing protein knots using knotoid theory, a framework that accounts for open curves in three-dimensional space. Our research proposes a systematic method for computing a knotoid invariant known as the 5-voltage value, which can be used to evaluate the equivalence of curves and identify patterns among a group of proteins. By examining voltage values under the influence of various reparameterization and deformation rules, we aim to uncover hidden similarities and structural features within protein populations. As a case study, our approach is applied to analyze a collection of 21 knotted and preknotted protein samples, yielding insights into their underlying topology and folding behavior.

To resolve the discrepancy known as the Hubble tension, early dark energy (EDE) has been proposed. Although researchers agree on the existence of EDE, its properties remain unclear. By analyzing the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's large-scale structure, we discovered a significant inconsistency in constraints when compared to each other, indicating possible evidence of an inconsistency when considering the cosmic background, large-scale behavior, and nuclear oscillations simultaneously. This discrepancy indicates that the core physical properties of early dark energy, such as when it first appears, how much it influences the universe's expansion, and when it disappears, need to be determined with greater precision.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite.

A detailed examination of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematics. This study leverages the Heisenberg uncertainty principle to explore various aspects, uncovering a link between the anomalous NG theorem and the Heisenberg uncertainty relation following symmetry breakdown. It also reveals that the ratio of vacuum expectation values for certain operators is governed by the uncertainty relation, further discovered is that the Mermin-Wagner theorem is interconnected with the anomalous NG theorem, ultimately finding that the anomalous NG theorem can be interpreted as a manifestation of the combined Heisenberg and Mermin-Wagner theorems. This analysis is conducted using a framework built upon operator algebra, leading to an algebraic understanding of the Mermin-Wagner theorem, which serves as a general inequality that holds for operators affected by symmetry breaking, confirming that both the Mermin-Wagner and anomalous NG theorems are interconnected expressions of uncertainty and commutation relations arising from symmetry breaking.

Recent studies have utilized counterfactual data, slightly modified versions of images, to enhance the efficiency of machine learning models. These machine-learning models are trained in a supervised manner and assign labels to data. However, there is limited public access to counterfactual datasets suitable for machine learning. This study introduces the DISCO framework, which generates high-quality counterfactual images from real images and can be customized based on the attribute of interest, allowing for efficient production of large-scale counterfactual datasets. The experiments demonstrate that utilizing these counterfactual datasets in machine learning models results in improved model performance and reduced cost through counterexample-based feedback, which provides counterfactual images along with a counterexample label for each data sample during machine learning training.

In this study, we determined the total chromatic numbers along with their equitable and
neighborhood sum distinguishing counterparts for specific types of circulant graphs.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene has primarily focused on elements with similar lattice sizes to graphene's parent substrate. Conversely, we discovered that certain Heusler compounds can be grown via remote epitaxy on graphene/Al2O3(0001) using this method. Specifically, for materials like CoFeAl, our findings revealed the absence of epitaxial alignment with the underlying substrate, yet a distinct fourfold symmetry was evident in the LeBail refinement of the diffraction pattern. Moreover, the analysis of the Heusler layer showed a 45 degree rotation, and the detection of a superlattice peak at 0.025 degrees confirmed the presence of a graphene buffer layer through the use of remote epitaxy.

A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code under specific conditions related to $p$. In this paper, an approach is proposed to determine the distance of the code obtained from the Gray mapping process. Additionally, a method is described to identify the subcode responsible for defining the $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code that produces a $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear code through the Gray mapping process. As examples, code parameters are calculated for a few code cases, and code dimensions are determined for all code parameters in size 4 and 8 when $p=3$.

The technology of graded viscosity banks, specifically tapering for polymer flooding,
has been analyzed using various models of mixing zone behavior. By considering different
viscosity functions, researchers have mathematically determined the optimal polymer injection
profile, given transverse flow equilibrium assumptions, for both the Koval and Todd-Longstaff models.
Moreover, a numerical assessment has been conducted to evaluate potential polymer gains relative
to flooding using a finite number of polymer slugs.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in generating realistic data from various conditions across multiple domains. However, the lack of rigorous quantitative evaluation and standardized benchmarks in this field hampers meaningful comparison of models and the development of evaluation tools tailored to specific tasks and metrics. In this study, we introduce a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of six cGAN models across three diverse tasks: synthetic image synthesis, natural language generation, and audio production. Our results, consisting of over 200 results and 100+ quantitative metrics, provide a means for researchers to meaningfully compare models on specific tasks and datasets. Additionally, we release evaluation scripts and results to facilitate the replication of our experiments and the creation of new evaluation metrics. Our findings offer valuable insights for the cGAN community and can guide the development of new models and tasks.

This study investigates the property of energy dissipation associated with the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation, introducing an upper bound that decreases over time, aligns with the original energy at time zero and as time approaches infinity. The upper bound can be perceived as a nonlocal-in-time modified energy, which includes both the original energy and a cumulative component stemming from the memory effect of the time-fractional derivative. Specifically, it demonstrates that the original energy actually declines as time passes in a localized area near the immediate past. Although the proof for the model equation is primarily focused on, the underlying argument can be applied to a broader class of subdiffusion models with corresponding modified energies.

Let A be a universal concrete C*-algebra, we demonstrate that the collection of all possible GNS representations generated by applying the GNS construction to individual states on A, is exhaustive - meaning it contains every possible C*-representation of A.

The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic models, where a jet of particles from the central supermassive black hole impacts the surrounding environment and generates a relativistic jet, are the leading explanation for this phenomenon.  The relationship between the energy of gamma-rays and the rate at which matter enters the black hole is currently under investigation through two methods: using external photon energy and gamma-ray photons that interact with each other (pair-thick jets).  Researchers have discovered that a specific range of accretion rates between 10^-3 and 10^-2 times the critical rate are ideal for producing gamma-rays through both methods.  However, when the accretion rate exceeds this range in either direction, at least one of the methods becomes ineffective.  The behavior of the most gamma-ray active sources, such as M87, MG 0111+DEC 373, and OJ 287, with an accretion rate similar to that of ESO 246-49 4, suggests that pair-thick jets may be more common than thin jets.  These findings offer a new perspective on the connection between the matter entering the black hole and the gamma-rays it produces, and may aid in understanding the behavior of hadronic jets and the origin of gamma-rays in such galaxies.

This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of the probability function, including higher-order moments, in a single calculation. Additionally, an explicit solution to the inverse function is provided, and key results are adapted to options pricing for both European and American styles. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of our methods through numerical experiments, highlighting their performance in solving portfolio problems and option pricing scenarios.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like auscultation are vital for this purpose. While some advanced technology can aid diagnosis, auscultation remains an effective and cost-free method that leverages human expertise. To improve this process, deep learning has been investigated, but many relevant datasets are either costly to acquire or lack diversity in terms of patient demographics. We have assembled a comprehensive dataset for auscultation analysis at no cost, comprising 1250 audio samples from 500 patients of varied ethnic backgrounds. This dataset is accompanied by detailed documentation of its collection, processing, and annotation process, and is intended to aid in the early and accessible diagnosis of heart conditions through auscultation.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices has facilitated enhanced health monitoring, enabling real-time data analysis and effective disease prevention. Despite these advancements, significant challenges persist in efficiently monitoring individual health through wearables. The primary issues lie in managing the vast amounts of data generated by these devices and customizing their functionality to suit each user's unique needs. The problem is further complicated by the slow speed and limited capacity of wireless communication protocols used to transfer data to mobile devices. To overcome these limitations, a new approach utilizing Body Area Network and a machine learning-based method is proposed in this study. By analyzing the varying sampling rates and communication speeds of Bluetooth Low Energy, a proposed system optimizes data transfer speeds and storage, effectively reducing the load on mobile devices and wearable units. Furthermore, an automatic configuration approach based on wearables' capabilities, available software resources, user preferences, and real-time health data is used to provide optimal system settings and user-specific health insights. The approach was tested and validated using a variety of devices and scenarios, yielding improved accuracy (95%) when compared to the alternative method, along with reduced data transfer times and storage space.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations.

In string compactifications, we suggest that dark energy marks the universe's end, 
potentially triggered by decompactification or vacuum decay, which could be explained 
through the cosmological swampland conjectures. We focus on heterotic string theory 
on $T^6$/$(S^4)^2$, deriving a constraint on the dark energy density parameter, $\Omega_{DE}$, 
and volume V as V$\times$(e$^{-60}$ - e$^{-10}$). Using a slow-roll inflation model, 
we find the initial extra-dimensional volume parameter $v_0$ ranges between 10$^{6.5}$ and 10$^{10.5}$, 
consistent with current data, indicating that Hubble scale inflation leads to a stable 
our-verse vacuum with positive V-energy equivalent to the observed dark energy density. 
This supports the hypothesis that our universe may expand forever.

In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing a substantial number of applicants, a time-consuming and intricate process. To achieve efficiency, a well-planned approach to selection is crucial. This process comprises multiple, interconnected problems, each mirroring a complex issue. Due to the absence of established data sets, developing a process for creating instances that reflects real-world scenarios proves challenging. In this study, we address this challenge by presenting a method for generating instances for a specific problem encountered during interview scheduling. We also discuss potential applications of these generated instances and present solutions for each.

This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Alongside, we examine the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a system of stochastic differential equations featuring abrupt obstacles, whose characteristics depend on the unknown solution. Finally, the paper also considers the case when the underlying system includes a random movement, resulting in the optimal payoff becoming a solution to a quasi-variational HJB PDE system with discontinuous barriers. This research is an extension of prior works on smooth costs in references [8, 17].

To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates asymmetric leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and aid in identifying its potential. Asymmetric production stands out from conventional methods as leptoquarks created in proton-proton collisions aren't opposite charges. To make this process possible, we outline the required conditions and list all relevant combinations of leptoquark groups that can create it. Furthermore, our studies in the Standard Model and its scalar extensions demonstrate how to integrate this process into reinterpretations of existing experiments, producing more accurate leptoquark property constraints.

Temporal sequence data is extensively studied, but current methods like Hidden Markov Models and Long Short Term Memory networks often struggle to balance interpretability and performance. A recently proposed approach, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time (SGTM-TT), builds on traditional autoencoders by creating a visually organized, semantic-preserving low-dimensional representation of complex temporal patterns, allowing for the exploration of temporal data from both global and local perspectives. By examining the connections between encoded representations and original sequences, as well as between time-step dependent representations, researchers can gain a comprehensive understanding of the intricate dynamics present in Complex Lissajous Curve Generation (CLLCG) and other complex time-series datasets. Not only does our study demonstrate the versatility of TLM, but it also highlights the potential of using Variational Autoencoders (VAE) as an alternative, providing the basis for a publicly accessible code repository and dataset.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which we had spectroscopic data of two specific fine structure lines from a carbon atom. This analysis allowed us to estimate the excitation conditions of molecular gas in these instances. Our results showed that most carbon atoms were highly excited, with exceptions noted in local group galaxies and some low-metallicity galaxies. This excitation state has implications on gas temperature estimates and the interpretation of carbon emission lines. Our analysis showed that carbon lines may not always be an indicator of ionized gas, especially in regions with high temperatures. This line's behavior can be different from other similar lines, with the potential to indicate different conditions in various environments. This analysis has significance on non-equilibrium excitation conditions and the interpretation of similar lines in similar situations.

We tackle current, striking discrepancies in flavor anomalies observed within the $K$ and $B$ meson systems, specifically addressing CP-violating Kaon decay and lepton-flavor universality violation in $B$ meson decays, with the introduction of heavy vector-like quarks and flavon scalar field vacuum expectation values that differ by just two orders of magnitude. Furthermore, this approach naturally yields the desired heavy vector-like quark masses and ensures the stability of the electroweak Higgs potential through new scalar interactions.

Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 1985 with a different formulation than the version we consider here. In our definition, the number of duplication patterns is fixed at one, followed by a different way to copy the duplicated segment. A transmitted sequence is called reconstructible if its original form is uniquely determined from its derived copies. In this study, we determine the minimum number of duplication patterns required for a transmitted sequence to be recoverable. We also find the minimum number in relation to the length of the transmitted sequence, its alphabet size, and other relevant parameters. Additionally, our results for the original problem are obtained as a consequence of our main findings.

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks for musical instrument identification by adding a priority module to the hierarchy-based process. This innovative approach enables efficient use of cross-class information in identifying similar instruments. We validate our proposed method on two datasets, CrossTab and musical instrument identification with protoPiano. In musical instrument identification with few shots (protoPiano), our model significantly outperforms other identification strategies, especially when there are very few examples to work with, achieving a top-5 accuracy of 61.5% at 5 shots and 51.3% at 2 shots, respectively, when using priority-enhanced prototypes.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper components. Developing effective Question Answering tools is hindered by the absence of large datasets that capture interactive needs for information between humans and researchers when analyzing research findings. We introduce a Question Answering dataset called Dialog-based Multi-hop (DM-HQAD) derived from over 11,000 research papers and containing 29,000 questions, where each question's answer relies on component relationships that are also present in the paper. The DM-HQAD dataset is unique as it captures the actual information needs of research paper readers, including their interactive and iterative questioning process. We develop a method that leverages the rich component features of the DM-HQAD dataset, incorporating both textual and structural information, and achieve a result of 31.5% in micro-F1 that outperforms baseline models.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for PTA data analysis. Furthermore, we introduce an improved version of these expressions that significantly minimizes computational errors and associated uncertainties. The findings also reveal that the majority (around nine-tenths) of previously computed mismatch values between the original and improved expressions fall below 10^-9, effectively negligible for PTA data analysis. The enhanced formulas are now publicly accessible through the GUPPI software.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalised models, considering applications such as the epidemic's progression, the incorporation of multiple compartments, the inclusion of population demographics, the integration of spatial factors, the consideration of population behavior, and the impact of control measures. A key emphasis is placed on model authenticity through the use of stochastic processes. Our analysis also explores numerical solution techniques and theoretical properties of model dynamics, including stability and coexistence of multiple equilibrium states. The discussion culminates in an examination of model applications and suggestions for future research directions.

We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we develop a Majorana fermionic gas subject to a semi-infinite Fermi gas profile in an one-dimensional system. Calculating the entropy per particle reveals how the gas's behavior is influenced by the strength of the Fermi gas profile and the Majorana mass.

Acronyms serve as a vital means of abbreviation in written language, but their interpretation poses a significant obstacle in text preprocessing, compilation, and comprehension. Due to the infinite nature of acronyms and the scarcity of comprehensive, high-quality datasets in this domain, effective acronym-based text representation models have yet to emerge. This study presents a novel, systematic approach for collecting acronym expansion data through a web-crawling technique that automatically gathers data from diverse, real-world sources. Our method yields the largest publicly available dataset comprising over 10 million samples, which after thorough verification and de-duplication, results in a high-quality dataset comprising nearly 3.5 million entries. Experimental outcomes, conducted in cooperation with natural language processing models, demonstrate that this dataset can significantly enhance model performance on acronym expansion tasks, particularly in scenarios where models are asked to generate multiple possible expansions for a single entry.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met, or when the system is not exactly balanced, leading to potential three-body separation or conversion from excited states. We also explored whether a specific dark-state resonance can be achieved even when the system is not precisely balanced.

Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects through a shared address space based on object names. This architecture enables efficient data object segmentation and modification by identifying and removing specific parts based on the structure itself. By facilitating the preservation of commonly named object segments, it significantly reduces redundancy. Furthermore, it naturally supports a flexible content-addressable storage system and effectively minimizes the flat look-up method's overhead. Similar to self-organizing memory cells found in synapses, it provides a robust framework for implementing peer-to-peer cache structures. Our systematic evaluation of over 10^12 objects demonstrates that this architecture requires only a minimal increase in look-ups while offering a flexible hierarchy for both data organization and reduction of duplicate content.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, exhibiting exceptional properties such as robust quantum Hall effects, unusual scattering behaviors, and exceptional capacitance in metallic structures. Although these properties are well-documented, they primarily rely on the impact of disorder and the distinction between bulk and surface characteristics. By leveraging the graphical notation of non-interacting many-body quantum systems, this study reveals a new class of topological matters – edge matters – that emerge even in perfectly ordered two-dimensional models and result in unique one-dimensional properties. These properties include distinct correlation patterns between opposite charges, photon scattering effects, and unique entanglement characteristics. This research also establishes a link between this novel edge matter and traditional one-dimensional topological insulators.

A brain tumor affects every age group and has no gender preference for occurrence.
A tumor is a serious illness that can arise in any part of the brain.
When it comes to detecting and diagnosing brain tumors, MRI is the primary and most widely used method.
In this study, we used the Unet architecture along with several optimization techniques to process MRI images and identify brain tumors.
Specifically, we explored three optimization algorithms and conducted experiments using the public available UHMRIs dataset.
As a result, our best configuration achieved a remarkable 97.2% accuracy in identifying brain tumors, outperforming other Unet variations and confirming its effectiveness in this task.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility or spatially discretized lighting models, resulting in poor quality synthetic images. In response to these limitations, VisionStokes introduces light transport visualization into the differentiable rendering process and employs the discrete spherical harmonics expansion to optimize lighting conditions for quality image synthesis. Experimental results demonstrate that utilizing VSH enables simultaneous improvement in image synthesis performance and a significant reduction in optimization time when compared to both harmonic and visibility-based bases, particularly when optimizing for complex lighting scenarios.

A popular technique, widely used in video technology over the last few decades, is interlacing. This technique splits each frame into two half-frames, or fields, captured at staggered times with half the total resolution. Thanks to the high temporal frequency of fields, motion appears smoother, especially at lower frame rates, making interlacing appealing. However, this approach introduces artifacts during high motion scenes, necessitating deinterlacing to produce a final frame. Existing deinterlacing methods face challenges balancing the trade-off between computational cost and visual quality. In contrast, our proposed approach, leveraging benefits from convolutional neural networks (CNNs), employs a single CNN network to deprocess both fields into a single frame, outperforming competing deinterlacing solutions in terms of quality. Furthermore, this method eliminates processing asymmetry, as both fields are treated equally with the same network, and our experiments demonstrate that our solution excels even when field labels are reversed.

The investigation revealed a disparity of approximately 0.1 fm in the root mean square radius of the neutron point distribution between non-relativistic mean field models and their relativistic counterparts. Further analysis revealed the discrepancy arises due to varying product values of the effective mass and one-body potential strength within the respective frameworks, with those values being governed by the Hugenholtz-Van Hove theorem. In contrast, the thickness of the neutron skin was found not to solely correlate with the symmetry potential but rather was heavily dependent on the nucleon effective mass.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks, controlling flow in hydraulic structures, and studying river dynamics. Although it's possible to model these predictions using the Shallow Water Equations, traditional numerical methods like Finite Volume, despite their accuracy, can be computationally expensive. To address this challenge, our research explores the use of finite element-based tree structures and machine learning algorithms to solve these equations and develop a predictive model for river flow velocities. By leveraging the capabilities of XTensor and the tree-based accelerator architecture, we created a highly efficient river flow velocity prediction accelerator called RiverFlowX. By integrating a tree-based solver and a machine learning predictor, RiverFlowX leverages the processor's capabilities to deliver real-time, accurate predictions for 3D river flow velocities. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, with a predictor accuracy of around 94% and a 4x speedup in real-time predictions when using a 100 million data point training set. Additionally, RiverFlowX achieves a 1.5x speedup over the original GPU implementation, providing a robust and efficient solution to real-time river flow velocity predictions.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at different exposures
to compensate for a lens's limitations in simultaneously recording very bright
and dark areas. This allows for an accurate recording of an scene's overall
brightness variation, which can span several orders of magnitude. This
capability is essential for replicating human vision in computational
imaging systems. In this study, we present a computational HDR method
utilizing only a single image, which is possible due to the significant
variation in brightness across different parts of an scene. We introduce a
learning-based approach to determine the scene's dynamic range by analyzing
the HDR properties of natural images. This novel method leverages a pre-trained
network, trained on synthetic HDR data, to estimate the HDR characteristics
of a given image. The method is unique in that it does not rely on any
capturing devices beyond the camera used to capture the image, which is
necessary for obtaining the required metadata. This approach is distinct
in that it does not rely on any capturing devices beyond the camera used to
capture the image, which is necessary for obtaining the required metadata.

Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of methods within the field. A new perspective on causal deep learning is presented, focusing on specific methods that can be effectively applied to particular problems, thereby facilitating the development of new approaches and enhancing future research directions, such as benchmarking and standardization.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings in these systems is often difficult or impossible due to their opaque nature. Our research proposes a novel non-invasive method for measuring reactor temperature using optical tomography, inspired by medical imaging techniques. For this approach to succeed, it's essential to develop a non-absorbing material capable of withstanding high temperatures, replacing the traditional catalytic packing. Our simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in reconstructing both uniform and non-uniform temperature distributions, even in the absence of complete knowledge regarding the reactor's refractive properties. Our findings suggest that this technique could successfully monitor temperature changes in real-time within catalytic fixed bed reactors, providing a means for optimizing and overseeing reaction conditions.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle for directions of principle one. It demonstrates that the broken submersions category is equivalent to the Janus map functions, which in turn is divided into two smaller groups: the Yoneda and the anti-Yoneda. It also establishes that the broken submersions category is analogous to its directed counterpart, which has applications in showing that two theories are theoretically identical.

This research involves solving complex problems related to the mechanics of the heart by applying mathematical techniques from continuum mechanics and numerical analysis. Two specific approaches, a block Jacobi-SOR and a new two-way block alternating method, are evaluated and compared based on their effectiveness when using a common preconditioning technique. Using a finite element model of a realistic heart model, the study indicates that the new alternating method outperforms the block Jacoco-SOR preconditioner by around 40% in computational speed.

The standard normalized form of a semi-circular distribution's density function is density(x) = \frac{2}{\pi} \sqrt{1-x^2} for values within the range [-1,1]. When considering an $n$-by-$n$ symmetric matrix $A$ with entries a_{ij} that are independently drawn from a standard normal distribution, the trace of the matrix multiplied by itself at power $k$, denoted as m_k(A) = \frac{1}{n^{k/2}}\sum_{i_1,...,i_k=1}^n A_{i_1i_2}...A_{i_ki_{k+1}}, converges to the $k$-th moment of the semi-circular distribution as $n$ increases, for odd values of $k$. However, when $m_k(A)$ is redefined with a different prefactor, denoted as M_k(A), a different behavior is observed with limiting values equal to the $k$-th moment of the standard normal distribution. Moreover, a key property is identified with a non-crossing pair-partition set, den as NC_2(k), that plays a crucial role in achieving this limiting behavior as $n$ becomes large. Additionally, a hybrid random variable is identified whose distribution can be expressed as a product of two independent variables, one following a semi-circular distribution and the other following a standard normal distribution, with a multip

Persuasive promotional videos, created with the intention of influencing opinions or prompting actions, are made frequently by both businesses and individuals.  Consequently, there is a growing need for innovative techniques that enable more efficient and accessible creation of these influential videos.  To achieve this, we establish a framework for producing persuasive videos on social media topics through a defined process.  This process involves carefully selecting a cause, crafting an engaging narrative, and refining the final video to maximize its influence.  We leverage artificial intelligence to streamline each step, beginning with a novel approach called CauseR to facilitate causal dialogue and enhance decision-making, followed by the development of a structured framework for efficient video production, and concluding with the application of the R-Net for minimal feedback needed to generate highly persuasive content, as demonstrated in our experiments.

Recent studies have uncovered the prevalence of gradient masking in purportedly robust adversarial defenses. Consequently, defense strategies based on this concept are considered ineffective and can be readily bypassed. Notably, research into quantifying the occurrence and extent of gradient masking across different networks remains limited. This study addresses this gap by exploring the mensurability of gradient masking as a multi-dimensional rather than a binary phenomenon. In addition, we introduce novel metrics designed to evaluate the presence of gradient masking in diverse neural networks. These proposed metrics not only offer computational advantages but also facilitate comparative assessments between models. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the efficacy of our approach in gauging the prevalence of gradient masking, thereby providing a more nuanced understanding of the phenomenon across different neural network architectures.

In recent years, research into complex periodic structures has gained momentum due to their ability to manipulate sound effectively. A specific type of acoustic metamaterial, known as bianisotropic, has shown promise for manipulating wave scattering in two dimensions, although its practical realization has been limited by difficulties in creating acoustic components that possess the necessary properties. Overcoming these challenges, we have developed a high-performance acoustic metagrating consisting of simple bars that can efficiently transfer incident sound waves to specific regions, appearing as if they were a single point source. This metamaterial has the potential to revolutionize applications, such as concentrating ultrasound on moving targets and creating acoustical cloaking devices. The success of our design relies on the utilization of large amplitude scattering inherent in acoustic physics, enabling us to achieve optimal performance at levels of pressure significantly greater than those typically used in such research. As a result, our metagrating design represents a major advancement in the field of acoustic metamaterials, paving the way for practical real-world implementations.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. In the case of stationary fractional Brownian motion, this analysis simplifies into a problem of determining the probability density function of a normal vector within a subspace, resulting in the identification of a specific manifold and various manifolds in relation to a given time period. We provide explicit formulas for these cases, including those involving orthogonal increments, and offer numerical solutions for scenarios lacking closed-form solutions, ultimately leading to a general conclusion for stationary processes.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators. This framework allows for a comprehensive examination of various phenomena, including solitons, bistability, bound states, and barcodes. By considering a general model of a planar resonator with two interacting modes, more specific applications are explored, including surface-emitting diode lasers and high-efficiency modulators based on nonlinear optics.

This paper builds upon established connections between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in control systems that allow unbounded controls, encompassing polynomial control systems. Our analysis specifically addresses unbounded open-loop controls and discontinuous feedback stabilizers, which may lead to trajectories exhibiting chattering behavior near the target. A central aspect of our findings is the demonstration of the equivalence between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in these control systems or their impulsive system extensions.

A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized for high-resolution velocity reconstruction, with the assessment of its effectiveness being performed through direct numerical simulation data for turbulent flow with longitudinal obstacles at different Reynolds numbers. The evaluation showed that this deep learning framework accurately replicates high-resolution velocity patterns and statistical measures from two low-resolution data sets. Furthermore, it was observed that this model successfully recreates turbulent velocity patterns at Reynolds numbers that it was not originally trained on.

The paper addresses misconceptions surrounding Jefimenko's equations, which are derived from Maxwell's equations, for a specific charge and current configuration obeying the continuity equation. It subsequently derives a non-radiative condition across inertial frames, consistent with the stability requirements of an atom, and establishes that this condition is analogous to certain relationships between charge, current, and the wave equations. The paper then demonstrates that these relationships lead to quantised electromagnetic field energy displaying the characteristics of the Balmer series.

The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often make过分高的自信预测. This problem is exacerbated when the training data contains a class分布不匀的问题. To tackle this challenge, our proposed method, known as Confidence Calibration for Imbalanced Data (CC2ID), aims to adjust both过高的自信预测和不准确的自信预测. By employing K-nearest neighbors to调匀的邻居比例来估计边际调整因子, we can effectively校准模型预测. Our实验结果表明，CC2ID outperforms several现有的方法 in 多种场景下.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, many applications remain limited due to the lack of robustness when encountering new environments. When deployed in unstructured settings, agents often struggle with significant changes, resulting in poor performance. There is an pressing need to enhance the reliability of reinforcement learning systems when deployed in diverse and unpredictable real-world scenarios. This paper proposes using reinforcement learning combined with world knowledge in the form of logical constraints to ensure that learned policies remain aligned with fundamental principles. By integrating these constraints, the policy learning problem can be formulated as a constraint satisfaction problem, allowing for both offline and online validation of learned principles. Initial results show that this approach enables the development of reliable systems capable of operating in complex, unpredictable settings such as traffic rule learning and application.

Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Our approach and associated test data are available online.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden shift from localization to non-localization. Our theory and experimental results indicate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light localization can transition back to non-localization at higher quasiperiodic modulation strengths for some states, representing an unusual phenomenon. Additionally, this occurrence can be understood through a mathematical model that represents dimerized interactions over extended distances.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck Adaptive Optics system to enhance its capabilities. Currently under construction, Liger will be available to observe wavelengths between 0.96 micrometers and 2.5 micrometers with high sensitivity. However, Liger's full potential cannot be realized without comprehensive observational testing. To address this need, we are developing observation proposals tailored for Liger's development phase. These proposed configurations will allow for efficient evaluation of the system's performance, leveraging its key features such as multiple observing modes, high sensitivity, and the ability to detect faint objects. Successful system testing is crucial to ensuring Liger's ability to fulfill its scientific objectives.

In optical systems, resolving the relative positions of two point sources separated by a very small distance is significantly restricted due to diffraction, a phenomenon known as Rayleigh's curse. Researchers have successfully bypassed this limitation in phase retrieval algorithms by exploiting prior phase information, although these methods require extensive data and complex calculations. Here, we present a straightforward method that bypasses Rayleigh's curse in phase retrieval for two point sources, requiring only one intensity measurement and simple comparisons, again at the expense of increased data quantity. Notably, this algorithm can determine the sources' locations to a subwavelength precision under suitable conditions, specifically when the ratio of distance between the two targets and their distance from the detector screen is sufficiently large. Although it appears that our subwavelength resolution method has broad applicability, further analysis shows that it functions effectively even in the case of two targets located on the same plane.
This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties.

In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning signs of sudden, large-scale fluctuations is essential. Researchers are currently exploring methods to predict chaotic, irregular oscillations, including mixed-mode oscillations (MMOs) and chaotic behavior in mixed trajectories. This paper analyzes the modified Lotka-Volterra model that exhibits MMOs through an invariant curve and demonstrates a technique for detecting them. Specifically, we developed an approach to identify indicators of MMOs by examining time-series data and looking at the relationship between the two populations. This method is then applied to a dataset obtained from an experimental lake ecosystem consisting of two connected compartments, with one containing algae and the other a protozoan population feeding on the algae. Our analysis shows clear evidence of mixed-mode patterns, with warning signs of MMOs being accurately detected by both proposed approaches.

Determining whether bulge growth occurs primarily through mergers or internal processes is a key question in galaxy evolution. We examine the time-dependent, two-dimensional specific star formation rate map of 12 local group spiral galaxies using non-parametric modeling to investigate this further. Our analysis shows a consistent pattern of low specific star formation rates at the galaxy centers, which can be described by a characteristic length scale. We discovered a relationship between this scale and the galaxy's structural index, indicating that galaxies with more bulge-like structures have smaller scales. This is significant because it suggests a possible connection between a galaxy's structure and its star formation activity, which has not been thoroughly investigated so far.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news articles as
expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a dataset from
Slovene. The underlying model is a pre-trained multilingual BERT model, which
was either adapted to a zero-shot or few-shot setup by replacing its final
classification layer. The results from a few-shot and one-shot scenarios are
also compared against traditional methods using a linear classifier on the
Slovene sentiment-labeled dataset. The study's findings are positive, showing
that a few-shot approach successfully captures the intended sentiment even
without explicit labels. The successful method outperformed the one-shot
alternative. Notably, the best-performing few-shot method achieved a F1 score
of 0.732, indicating a certain level of accuracy in detecting the article's
true sentiment. This result is comparable to the F1 score of 0.75 obtained by
the one-shot approach. The study's positive outcome has significant practical
implications, as it demonstrates that sentiment op-ed articles can be effectively
categorized as positive, negative, or neutral based on the emotion they
convey, utilizing data from three major sources including Facebook, even in
situations where the article's sentiment is not explicitly stated.

Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen program behaviors. In response, we introduce a formal framework for analyzing program semantics with the issue of store buffer and coherence, and we integrate this with DCEM, a representative protocol. With this theoretical foundation, we devise an interprocedural analysis method to pinpoint and expose violations of memory safety, correctness issues, and performance problems. We then extend this framework to support spinlock-based programs using a specific example of DCEM. Through extensive experiments, we show that our approach can address issues in various benchmark cases and custom spinlock programs after applying the program semantics with relaxed memory ordering. Additionally, our analysis yields improved program performance in multiple examples.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions.

Consider a fractional Brownian motion $B^{H}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with Hurst index $H$ in the interval $(0,1)$. Let $f$ be a Borel function from $[0,1]$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and $A$ a Borel subset of $[0,1]$. Conditions will be established under which the image $(B^{H}+f)(A)$ has a positive Lebesgue measure or a non-empty interior. This is achieved through investigating properties of the occupation measure corresponding to $(B^{H}+f)$, including proving that certain sets within the graph of $f$ possess a specific Hausdorff dimension, homeomorphic sets, and determining that the density function of the occupation measure belongs to a specific $L^{p}$ space, where $p$ is determined by $H$.

Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we establish a simple H\'enon-Heiles model based on semiclassical mechanics. A two-body trial wavefunction in the form of Hatree-type is applied, leading to the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian in the context of Jackiw-Kerman theory. The calculations yield results indicating that quantum fluctuations can provoke chaotic behavior in regions of the H\'enon-Heiles system that classically remain stable.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics, or semantic features, that have been shown to correlate with patient disease progression and clinical status in patients with COVID-19. Prior research has attempted to detect these features and build predictive models for severe symptoms based on them. However, there is still lack of a well-curated, annotated dataset linking specific visual patterns in the images to their clinical meanings. In this work, we introduce such a dataset, consisting of 1274 chest radiographs from patients with COVID-19, where doctors annotated severe symptoms correlates in the images and also linked them to patient history and outcome. We also propose a method for extracting these features and experimented on them in various ways to predict severe symptoms, thereby contributing images' interpretations to the dataset. We also make our dataset publicly available for others to build upon.

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C elevates to a functors defined on the category of simplicial algebras in C to the category of universal algebras in the category of simplicial sets in C. This occurs when the variety A of algebras is such that it contains no non-trivial simplicial algebras defined on weakly contractible simplicial sets in C, provided the model structure on the category of simplicial sets in C is established using the varietopological functor V from the category of simplicial sets in C to the category of simplicial algebras in C. This condition is met for many varieties A of algebras, including group, ring, and Lie algebra varieties. Furthermore, if the model structure on the category of simplicial algebras in C is defined using the varietopological functor V from the category of simplicial sets in C to the category of simplicial algebras in C, this occurs when the variety A of algebras is such that it contains no non-trivial simplicial algebras defined on weakly contractible simplicial sets in C, and the class of weak equivalences is limited to acyclic simplicial algebras. This condition is met for some varieties A of algebras, although it excludes ring and Lie algebra varieties. This occurs when the model structure on the category of simplicial

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily classified due to their semantic distinctiveness. This VRD task difficulty stems from needing to predict low-frequency hard-to-predict relationships accurately. To address this, we developed a comprehensive dataset with annotated hard negative samples for each positive one. This dataset, called HeavyLight, significantly boosts the false positive rate in the vocabulary, making it challenging even for human annotators to differentiate some correct negative proposals. Two VRD models trained on this dataset consistently outperform previous state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining strong results.

This study offers an innovative approach to solving the problem of action recognition in images taken in the dark. By building upon a state-of-the-art action recognition system that utilizes visible light, we developed a framework that makes use of infrared and ambient light to improve performance in low-light conditions. This proposed method achieves remarkable results on the KiVi dataset, outperforming existing low-level image processing techniques and ensuring robustness against a diverse range of light conditions. By comparing our infraBIR proposal to the results of the KiVi challenge, we observed that the majority of the submitted solutions were not as effective as our approach, which was highlighted by the lack of action-related information in the infrared channel and the effectiveness of using the two input channels in an additive manner.

This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design uniquely captures Caxton C. Foster's pioneering ideas on parallel processing, incorporating the concepts of simultaneous parallel writes and the merging of output values – features commonly omitted in typical CAM applications like network routing. The resulting system allows a host computer to interface with the CAPP over USB/UART using a simple serial communication protocol, which has been effectively demonstrated through the creation of two computer interfaces: a Raspberry Pi in C and a PC in Python using a Virtual Serial Port Driver. Furthermore, we provide a thorough protocol specification, along with source codes for the Python driver and the C application, which have been made publicly available on GitHub.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=0.37$ in a cluster environment that possess lopsided disks and have suppressed star formation. We've discovered that the suppression can be partly attributed to a flow of gas towards these galaxies, caused by a significant inflow velocity of approximately $60$ $km/s$. This finding highlights the role of recent and potentially ongoing inflows in the evolution of massive galaxies within clusters.

We re-examine and revise the predictions of the Universal Texture Zero (UTZ) flavour model as initially presented in the study arXiv:1709.09769. The revision is motivated by new resonance flavour measurements and updated global analysis results. Specifically, we employ two- and three-resonance UTZ variants to determine precise UTZ parameters, including complex Yukawa couplings. Our findings demonstrate the viability of the UTZ framework in explaining observed flavour data, with significant contributions from -2π shift in leptonic phases that can be experimentally verified. Furthermore, our analysis reveals previously unexamined connections between重轻子 decay patterns and flavour data, with implications for future experiments such as FCC-ee and Belle II. Additionally, radiative corrections in the UTZ model lead to predictive structures resembling UTZ textures in lepton and qupton sectors, with potential observable consequences in scattering processes and D-meson decay rates.

We examine a specific nonlinear elliptic equation in R^N, where N is 5 or greater. No studies on the periodicity of its solutions have been done previously, so we explore related issues by making some key assumptions about a given function, Q(y), which is periodic and has a minimum value at zero. We demonstrate that numerous "bubbling solutions" for this equation exist and can be classified in a specific way when these conditions are met, resulting in some of these solutions maintaining the same symmetry as Q(y). Additionally, we find that "bubbling solutions" will not exist under alternative circumstances when Q(y)'s local minimum is not zero, based on an analysis of energy and related concepts like concentration and bubble interaction.

Current cutting-edge neural code models excel at generating individual code segments but often struggle with complex tasks, like entire function code production. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages static code analysis for weak supervision. Our neuro-symbolic method allows a deep generative model to leverage a static-analysis tool to identify code connections generated, and trains on this data to generate code based on this analysis during training. When tested on the task of creating full Java functions within existing classes, our results reveal our approach outperforms state-of-the-art transformer models and a method that tries to learn program meanings, exceling at error-free code production and matching actual code structure.

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant event on November 7, 2004, linked to a powerful X2.0 solar flare. Analysis of recorded data revealed neutron and gamma-ray measurements were taken during and shortly after this event, revealing an unexplained gamma-ray spectrum with 511-keV lines and features indicative of hydrogen and oxygen compounds produced by high-energy protons interacting with water molecules. Historically, similar events had been detected in lower-altitude locations in Japan and the U.S., prompting a call for more research into sndp occurrences at mid-latitude locations.

We have determined the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various configurations - scalar, vector, and tensor - and found the differences between their behavior in divergence-based and relaxation-time-approximation models. Our comparison also shows correspondence with first-order causal theories and highlights how a specific divergence-based model can predict damped tensor waves. This aligns with kinetic theory's results. It's interesting that both hydrodynamic and holographic fluids display similar properties. These findings reinforce the feasibility of using hydrodynamics to analyze gravitational waves and suggest that precision measurements of such waves could help us understand the nature of quark-gluon plasma.

Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or deep learning, can be computationally demanding and require significant storage, making them impractical for continuous applications. A simple, efficient solution is proposed: the Light Forest (LiForest) method, using an extremely basic data structure known as a 'Forest' to learn from continuous data and identify anomalies in real-time. LiForest achieves real-time processing on diverse datasets, including network traffic and sensor data, at a speed of roughly 10 times faster than existing approach, such as one based on deep learning and using the Long Short-Term Memory technique. LiForest requires negligible memory, making it possible to run on low-cost devices like a Raspberry Pi, demonstrating its suitability for diverse, resource-constrained environments.

A pivotal question arises in contemporary law: under what circumstances can a judicial authority force an individual to provide a password for a digital device? In the US, the third-party doctrine plays a significant role in determining when the Fifth Amendment's self-incrimination protections are applicable. However, recent cases have left the specific requirements for these circumstances open to interpretation. Some legal experts argue that the third-party doctrine should be revised to protect respondents from being forced to enter a password for a device they own. This paper investigates the feasibility of simulating such password entry using existing cryptographic techniques, such as commitment schemes, zero-knowledge proofs, and obfuscation, with the aim of developing methods that prevent courts from learning the content of the respondent's device while still allowing them to review the contents of another party's device in a trial.

We have developed a comprehensive model that enables simulation of the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) process. It can predict real-world observations and outcomes in scenarios involving linear channel loss, including the associated gain levels, error rates in different measurement bases, and final key rates. Our model is versatile and can be applied to various MDI-QKD implementations that employ convex source states or diverse coding techniques. As such, it is an invaluable resource for analyzing and evaluating the performance of different MDI-QKD protocols.

Researchers at Cornell University, led by Guy Melson from the Computer Science department, developed a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for solving Min-CSP problems with finite relational signatures. Their method builds upon techniques created in 2015 by the same group to establish PTAS for specific types of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) with equal variables. Melson and his team at the Cornell Theory Center further refined these 2015 results to create the current approach. This new method is notable for not employing any rounding of fractional solutions to integers, and it was initially outlined in preprint form before being formally published in the International Journal of Foundations of Computer Science in 2017. The research was supported by several institutions, including the Cornell Theory Center, the National Science Foundation, and the Office of Naval Research.

This study presents a novel, high-order numerical method for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under a constant diffusion term. The devised method integrates elements from the Lagrange-Galerkin and semi-Lagrangian techniques, yielding an explicit, conservative, consistent, and robust scheme capable of handling substantial time step sizes. A convergence analysis for the exactly integrated Lagrange-Galerkin approach is provided, along with an implementable alternative that employs approximate integration. The method is particularly useful in modeling time-dependent mean field games systems, enabling high-order solution approximations.

Recent analyses of lepton flavor universality (LFU) violating decays have suggested that new physics might exist beyond the Standard Model, potentially influencing multiple areas, including flavor and Higgs couplings. This study provides a unified description of such observations using a specific class of new physics models - two Higgs doublet models. By applying this approach, we derive a set of common parameters describing LFU violations in semileptonic decays and two important ratios in $B$-meson decays. Our analysis shows that the data can be reasonably well fit with slight deviations from standard LFU. Furthermore, our model serves as a clear example of how New Physics could simultaneously impact several areas and enables predictions for other semileptonic and flavor changing processes.

Advancements in machine learning, particularly deep neural networks (DNNs), have led to remarkable success in image recognition technology. However, using these models in life-critical scenarios necessitates a fundamental understanding of their operational mechanisms. Unfortunately, existing models like convolutional neural networks (CNNs) opaquely function, hindering this essential comprehension. Recent research has attempted to address this issue by developing approaches to distill knowledge from high-performance models into simpler, easily understandable models. Unfortunately, these methods often inaccurately capture the genuine decision-making process of complex neural networks, limiting their practical utility. In an effort to overcome these shortcomings, this research proposes a novel, iterative distillation framework that adapts the distillation process dynamically, ensuring an precise approximation of the original DNN's behavior. Through a basic mathematical argument, it establishes that this approach gradually minimizes the difference between the original and adapted transformations. Numerical experiments demonstrate that this framework excels in preserving performance and accuracy when applied to various image classification tasks.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9246783 exhibits a significantly higher surface rotation rate relative to its core, which is an unusual phenomenon. We uncover multiple coherent rotation periods in this star and signs of a faster rotating inner core, which may be responsible for the unusual magnetic activity seen in KIC 9246783. These findings suggest that there is still much to learn about the core dynamics of low-mass giant stars.

Fake news has become a significant issue on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and minimal effort required to create it. Although machine learning methods have been developed to identify counterfeit news, they often require substantial amounts of labeled data. Unfortunately, these methods struggle to effectively identify fake news about sudden events, frequently misclassifying them. Furthermore, fake news can promote controversial opinions, distort personal beliefs, and promote extremist ideologies. Given the nature of social media, where extreme opinions are more prevalent, this can have far-reaching implications. To address this challenge, we propose a new approach that leverages a few shot learning to recognize low-data available targets. Our method incorporates a new technique, prototype augmentation, to enhance the feature representation of targets. To further improve this, we suggest an ensemble framework that fuses enhanced features with bag-of-words to capture semantic semantics. Our comprehensive experiments on the TwitterMedics19 dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed approach, yielding significant enhancements in accuracy.

This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation with a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$. Our findings show that for a strong dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$, the equation is proven to be globally stable and well-behaved over time. On the other hand, in the absence of a strong dissipation term, we discover that even with a weak $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ term, the equation may become undefined within a finite time, given certain conditions. Our results are obtained through a combination of techniques, including energy methods, inequalities, and estimates related to the kernels of the singular integral operators $D$ and $\Lambda^{\alpha}$.

This paper investigates the age of information (AoI) in a discrete-time status updating system that employs the Ber/G/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that utilizing a two-dimensional state vector which simultaneously monitors AoI and packet age enables derivation of the stationary AoI distribution via analysis of a constituted stochastic process. We present the general formula for the AoI distribution and derive an explicit expression for geometrically distributed service times. A comparison between discrete and continuous AoI is provided, including mean values for the M/M/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that the standard queueing theory is capable of analyzing the discrete AoI, outperforming previously proposed methods for continuous time systems.

This work delves into various quantum algebras that arise from a special type of set-theoretic solution to the Yang-Baxter equation and their 'q-analogue' counterparts, also providing common characteristics that these algebras must follow, in doing so it particularly provides a detailed analysis of quasi-triangular quasi-bialgebras and their properties, and specifically shows how the set-theoretic solutions-based algebras and their counterparts share a common quasi-R-matrix, thereby allowing them to be described through the 'q-deformed' classical YB equation.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad.

Quantum tunneling phenomena occur on atomic scales in solids, but they can be
significantly amplified by precise doping of silicon with phosphorus.
We have developed a theoretical model to explore the interplay between quantum tunneling
and silicon's inert 3s electrons, focusing on two key applications:
