calculating the magnetic interaction between two electrons and determining the electron's
Dottis frequency.
For the magnetic interaction, we consider two cases: when the electrons are
separated spatially and when they are part of a pair.
We utilize a modified version of the Spontaneous Correlation Kinetic model,
adapted to account for electron-nucleus interactions, which allows us to
obtain results in line with previous calculations by Levitt and Houck.
We have also obtained new data for cases that were previously unexplored numerically.
When the electrons are close together, our model yields results that match those
obtained by Levitt and Valiev analytically.
For the electron's Korringa frequency, we have employed a gradual removal technique
based on the number of electrons, which offers advantages over other methods such as Hylleraas-Clark
and Bond Breakdown methods, leading to more accurate results at a lower computational cost.
We have found that using the Balance Method to determine the one-electron
basis functions results in more accurate frequency predictions compared to the standard
double-zeta basis functions.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully apply graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the relationship between an enzyme and its substrates. Specifically, we explore networks that model individual reaction units and examine their ability to generalize across various topologies. Our results highlight the conditions necessary for these enzyme-based networks to accurately mimic the dynamics of their underlying chemical dynamics. Furthermore, our research reveals that, although increasing the number of identical reaction units leads to improved accuracy, the precise configuration of the network's underlying topology has a more substantial impact on performance.

We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, they struggle with low data availability in the medical field. Although GANs have solved some issues related to limited data availability, training them still poses challenges due to the need for extensive computation and memory. Although two-stage GANs have reduced computation, they introduce new problems such as the difficulty of aligning medical images from different sources, which can affect treatment outcome analysis. To address these challenges, a novel two-stage U-Net-GAN framework is proposed, which enhances computation and memory while ensuring precise segmentation of medical images and accurate transformation of them.

Strong nonlocality, a phenomenon where systems demonstrate nonlocality without entanglement, can be seen in multipartite states with certain properties. Unextendible product bases (UPBs) have shown nonlocality without entanglement in previous research. However, many UPBs-based protocols are limited by the fact that local measurements are not entangling. To address this limitation, our research aims to identify minimal-size UPBs that possess strong nonlocality. We provide conditions for demonstrating strong nonlocality in UPBs and specifically in those with graphic stabilizers. Additionally, we explore this condition in the context of minimal-size UPBs in four-dimensional Hilbert spaces. By doing so, we find multiple minimal-size UPBs with strong nonlocality, some of which are constructed from triangles and quadrilaterals.

The speed at which massive satellite formations can be reconfigured has long been limited due to the extensive time required for individual units to shift positions. Addressing this issue, our proposed solution leverages coordinated movement to achieve significantly faster reconfiguration times. By exploiting the inherent delays between units in the formation, we aim to reduce the total movement time and cost. To accomplish this, we suggest using astrobots equipped with coordinated targets to reduce overall movement time and cost. Our approach yields smaller clusters in less time, although target assignment impacts coordinated performance due to increased movement costs. Proposed solution finds an optimal target assignment through a modified transshipment problem, ensuring all targets are covered and the total cost is minimized. Our method can be adapted to scenarios with diverse robot speeds and sizes, and tested success on hundreds of random problem sets with up to 500 astrobots. Our approach outperforms traditional methods, achieving median cost reductions of 22% and up to 94% in certain cases.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule, which can only be applied when its root predicate is already satisfied within a graph. These roots serve as a framework for GP 2 programs, enabling the creation of innovative analysis and verification techniques. Additionally, a generic correctness improvement method is presented, which automatically enhances time complexity from quadratic to linear for GP 2 programs within a specific category, including an example of a novel time-efficient algorithm for determining transitive closure within the language.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained significant traction recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step involves the creation of contrasting pairs or groups, with this step's outcome directly impacting the framework's overall success. Our research makes key contributions by proposing innovative strategies for contrast generation, with mathematical guarantees provided for these contributions' validity. These include contrastive group generation, contrast-enhancing network structures that prioritize more challenging samples, gradual contrastive learning, and a contrastive graph generation method. The framework's effectiveness and the proposed strategies' ability to enhance contrast quality are confirmed through experiments on multiple dimensionality reduction tasks and dataset evaluations. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate the superiority of contrast-enhanced and contrast-graph generation methods in the contrastive learning framework.

This study establishes the number of arcs in locally semi-symmetric graphs whose automorphism groups are non-abelian and quasiprimitive, establishing this count as either 0 or 2 through comprehensive classification approaches, also yielding minimum and maximum degree values as well as specific quorum group types on points within these graphs's stabilizers.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires modeling a substantial number of potential interactions. Despite this challenge, many practitioners only evaluate the marginal effects of individual categories, potentially missing out on the prevalence of rare categories that have significant implications. We propose an efficient method for identifying and modeling these uncommon categories by treating the identification of such categories as a latent variable, therefor avoiding an exhaustive search for the best model. We evaluate our method through various data sets and compare it to alternative strategies, finding that our approach yields a more effective model and can be trained substantially faster than competing methods.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive sentences, while simultaneously improving the ability of the LLMs to accurately utilize information from knowledge graphs during downstream tasks.

This article examines spatially nonlocal diffusion models, where interactions are limited to a finite distance $\delta$ and investigates how they are defined in a bounded area with various boundary conditions representing inhomogeneous data. We compare their solutions with classical PDE models under specific localization limits, as well as how reducing the nonlocal interaction parameter $\alpha$ influences behavior. Our findings are supported by analogous experiments conducted on a fixed domain.

When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the same optical centers. Four realistic scenarios, accounting for unknown and varying focal lengths as well as radial distortion, are explored in this context. Comprehensive testing of the proposed methods is conducted using synthetic scenes and over 5000 real images obtained from 360-degree video sources. Furthermore, an application demonstrating in-situ projection of panoramic images onto spheres utilizing the proposed algorithms is showcased. Results of the evaluation and application are presented.

Hanzer and Muić's work on degenerate Eisenstein series cancellations has been built upon, 
extending their method and outcome to a specific set of Eisenstein series, 
specifically those formed from the combinations of two Speh representations 
$\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$ in $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ for self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation $\tau$.

This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data from a primate brain region model of the ventral striatum. Employing a generalized linear model, we identify key local network drivers in Parkinson's disease brain regions, discovering that thalamic and cortical drive to the midbrain exhibit oscillatory patterns at specific frequencies. Furthermore, our model reveals that these oscillations can synchronize at slower speeds during Parkinson's disease, closely mirroring changes observed experimentally in a primate brain. Additionally, our model successfully replicates the effects of left-sided medication and deep brain stimulation on reducing or eliminating the slow oscillatory patterns characteristic of Parkinson's disease. Our findings provide theoretical support for current understanding of Parkinson's disease and its treatment, as well as suggest that specific brain region stimulation may be more effective than others.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
We propose a novel approach to weather detection using computer vision, which can be implemented with a single device and a basic camera.
To support this, we have created the 'RFS Dataset', a comprehensive weather detection and classification set containing four categories: Rain, Fog, Snow, and clear skies.
In an experiment, our deep learning-based camera system achieved a high accuracy rate of 97.4%, outperforming the accuracy of human drivers at 85%.

To address modeling long sequences effectively, we introduce a dual-path RNN architecture that employs two separate processing routes: a primary path for general features and a secondary cells-on-edge path that focuses on long-term sequence information. This secondary path explicitly tracks the beginning and end of speech signals, enabling a more precise understanding of time alignment. Our approach, driven by this extra information, facilitates a more effective classification of speech activity and, notably, enhances the performance of time-domain speech spectrum extraction by more than 2 dB. This method, which requires no pre or post-processing, outperforms comparable models across multiple datasets, without relying on position encoding or other external cues for time alignment.

A new statistics methodology is introduced to assess the differences between cosmological models based on the distribution of the turn-around radii of cluster halos. This methodology can be applied to distinguish models by analyzing the distribution of these radii, which is feasible to compute numerically. When evaluated using three-dimensionally simulated and two-dimensionally projected data from the IllustrisTorch cosmological models, the method effectively distinguishes between $\Lambda$CDM and $f(R)$ models with radii up to approximately 90 kpc, accounting for approximately 10% of the Hubble radius. The method also demonstrates the ability to differentiate models even when model parameters are slightly varied. It becomes less effective at larger radii due to increased statistical scatter caused by the influence of small-scale initial conditions. This methodology can be utilized to differentiate models when observational data becomes available in the near future. Such data will come from extremely large-scale surveys, such as those utilizing radio interferometry to observe at millimeter wavelengths or radio telescopes to detect radio emissions, in the coming decade.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise for refining the simulation of atmospheric convection in weather and climate simulations. A key factor in their success lies in properly defining the interaction between fluid components at a microscale, which is crucial for applying these models to a mesoscale. A newly devised energy-based approach ensures that energy is conserved across fluid interfaces, but so far, its impact on fluid dynamics, including convection, has not been thoroughly examined. A theoretical analysis and accompanying computer simulations reveal that an additional pressure term, which arises from surface tension effects, can be integrated into the force balance equation to predict how this influence manifests. A similar analysis can also be applied to the force of capillarity. To validate these predictions, a simplified two-fluid system was used in controlled numerical experiments, where the system was applied to a fluid mixing scenario involving a rising air bubble. A good match was achieved between the simulated bubble behavior and predictions derived from traditional methods, even in scenarios where the bubble is filled with a substance that varies its density as the temperature changes. These findings support the conclusion that defining fluid dynamics through a multi-fluid approach, where energy is conserved between fluid components, is feasible and can be a crucial step in enhancing the accuracy of convection simulations in weather and climate models.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced. With increased detector load, cooling capabilities must be appropriately managed. This paper introduces a cooling solution tailored for this upgraded module, allowing efficient temperature regulation, proper electrical grounding, and module stability. Furthermore, modules are secured against potential vibrations during particle beam operations, and optimized for compact packaging to maximize spatial efficiency within the detector.

A method is presented for computing the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral density from lattice QCD data, which remains gauge invariant. The proposed method is tested on the SU(2) glueball spectrum for specific quantum numbers and at varying lattice spacings. The study employs published data to determine the spectral density and the glueball spectrum. The results for the ground state mass are consistent with the conventional approach using exponential correlations. Additionally, preliminary indications of excited states within the spectrum can be derived from the spectral density.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we will explore the use of deep learning techniques for sentiment
classification, starting with an examination of several pretrained models, including Bidirectional
LSTM, Tfidf, and Elmo. We will then determine the efficacy of these models through
experimental analysis, ultimately determining the most suitable model for sentiment
prediction based on our findings.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in vacuum, resulting in a nonlinear effect where light influences light. To understand this field interaction in the vicinity of a black hole, researchers have developed an effective potential that accounts for the nonlinear effects, modifying the traditional geometric optics approach. This modified approach enables the prediction of light shadow variations in accordance with the mass, spin of the black hole, and the nonlinear parameter. Notably, a critical threshold exists where shadow fluctuations become excessively large, indicating possible phase transitions with significant implications for theoretical physics. Moreover, the effective potential can also be applied to investigate gravitational waves emitted by photons near the event horizon, further expanding our comprehension of particle behavior in the extreme environment of a black hole.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. This difficulty is further exacerbated when dealing with highly non-Gaussian states of light. Our proposed approach streamlines this process by directly recovering the Wigner function from the optical tomogram, bypassing intricate deconvolution techniques. One method we devise involves using the Maximum Likelihood Estimation to achieve a physically plausible reconstruction that is simpler and avoids potential artifacts. This simplified procedure is demonstrated for coherent states and non-classical states such as squeezed states and cat states, but can be applied more broadly. A comparable procedure for discrete-variable systems is also described.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant milestones, yet introducing certain characteristics like persona, ensuring content safety, or other essential features poses a considerable challenge. Traditional methods to incorporate such features typically require costly data annotation. This paper investigates a vital but under-explored dimension: enabling safe and character-driven conversations without such annotation. Focusing on a previously unexamined aspect, this study explores building a secure, persona-driven dialogue system capable of handling self-contradictory scenarios without such annotation. To that end, this research examines this dimension and addresses a practical but neglected concern, developing a safe, persona-driven system without such annotation by examining how such characteristic can be effectively enforced in open-domain dialogue systems. It investigates such an unexamined aspect and addresses a crucial but overlooked issue, enforcing such feature like persona and safety in open-domain dialogue systems without such annotation. It explores such an unexamined aspect and addresses such an important but neglected issue, enforcing persona and safety in open-domain dialogue systems without such annotation. It investigates such an unexamined aspect and addresses such an important but neglected issue, enforcing persona and safety in open-domain dialogue systems without such annotation.

Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing average treatment benefits and risks. Evaluating pesticide efficacy using confidence intervals and p-values can be misleading due to varying disease pressures, costs, and treatment costs across different trials. Although Bayesian methods offer a solution by providing updated estimates of disease pressure and treatment efficacy, collecting historical data for this purpose can be costly. A practical solution involves using existing data from previous trials to assess efficacy with minimal additional data collection. This approach was demonstrated through a case study using cranberry trials, where researchers compared two datasets with varying amounts of historical data to evaluate the benefits of sharing information among researchers. The results showed that using existing data can provide meaningful efficacy estimates with minimal additional data collection, especially when funding for new trials is limited.

360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences but
require significant bandwidth. A common approach to reduce this demand is to
transmit only the region of interest in these videos. To determine the most
relevant areas in these videos remotely, this research proposes an innovative
method utilizing deep learning to analyze and interpret user input and gaze
data from a limited dataset. Specifically, we examine the effectiveness of
deep learning models in predicting regions of interest in videos viewed on a
Virtual Reality platform called A Vr Tour. Our comparative analysis of several
popular vision-based attention models reveals that the Attention Network (ANet)
proposes the most effective method to identify regions of interest in such
videos.

Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling different types of equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations, mostly through a time-slice decomposition approach. This technique reduces the problem's complexity by breaking down two-dimensional tensor networks into one-dimensional components. However, these methods generally struggle with problems featuring a long-range correlation between spatial and temporal dimensions. This common limitation was overcome by a new type of hierarchical time discretization. In this approach, each level is connected to all other levels, causing the two-dimensional equilibrium and one-dimensional non-equilibrium scenarios and allowing for higher accuracy or reduced error. As a result, the asymptotic convergence rate was found to be $\mathcal{O}(1)$ for each increase in hierarchical level, making this method particularly applicable to problems where the correlation between equilibrium and non-equilibrium states is prevalent. This new approach was demonstrated in the simulation of DMRG equilibrium electronic structure as part of a larger drive-system out of initial nonequilibrium state.

We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces.

In this research, we establish a precise inequality relating anisotropic mean curvature and capacity in the anisotropic $ anisotropic \ m$-area formula. This implies the anisotropic Minkowski inequality, which is also derived from an anisotropic $\ m$-perimeter-to-capacity inequality. This anisotropic $\ m$-perimeter-to-capacity inequality is itself obtained from an anisotropic $\ m$-isoperimetric inequality. Additionally, our work in this research provides a lower bound for anisotropic $\ m$-Yau inequality, which is also derived from an anisotropic Minkowski inequality.

The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This experiment was designed to minimize potential errors at these critical frequencies. Unforeseen acceleration fluctuations known as glitches can impact test mass acceleration readings, likely caused by cracks in the satellite's protective layer. These events, which are relatively rare, can result in large acceleration jumps that affect data analysis. This paper presents a method to automatically identify and mark glitch events using multiple principles. The new algorithm can detect and flag nearly all significant glitches with a high degree of accuracy.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that such a system exists where the dimer can switch between an inactive state and a highly active state. We also investigate systems where the particles interact uniformly, finding two distinct outcomes: the dimer remains inactive in areas with large activity contrasts, or it becomes active if the contrast is low. Alternatively, it can coexist with an inactive state. We further examine how control over position and activity gradient orientation can be achieved through an external gradient.

The minimum strong shortest path cover with k-hops in a graph G is the smallest number of sets needed among all k-hops strong shortest path covers, where we also examine 2-hops covers for certain graphs and show the general k-hops cover problem is NP-complete.

The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations demonstrate how non-linear small-x saturation impacts shift the Borel plane's initial IR pole from $2/\beta_2$ to $1/\beta_2$, thereby changing the estimated uncertainty to approximately $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^2$ instead of $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^4$.

As the number of frogs per site grows, the frog model's behavior shifts from transient to recurrent on a d-ary rooted tree. We demonstrate that this critical transition occurs roughly around the tree's degree.

Highly sensitive applications requiring ultrafast photoresponse to magnetic changes are significantly enhanced by combining rare-earth transition metal alloys at the nanoscale with plasmonic nanoantenna arrays. Our research focuses on a specific alloy of FeNdGd and a modified bull's eye grating to achieve this goal. By utilizing a array-scan method, we demonstrated the capability to retrieve stored Faraday information with temporal resolution in the femtosecond range. Notably, our design enables FeNdGd to contribute to both near and far-field energy flow in the visible spectrum, resulting in a few percent modulation of Faraday signal over a few hundred femtoseconds. Additionally, this arrangement allows for reduced sample thickness while still effectively leveraging the coherent excitation of surface plasmon polaritons to maximize energy exchange. Furthermore, our work highlights the adaptability of this approach to other rare-earth doped alloys and the potential for optimizing performance through the customization of plasmonic resonances to match specific emission properties. This research has significant implications for the development of next-generation photonic devices with ultrafast magnetically controlled sensing capabilities.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible in practical scenarios involving proprietary models or cloud services. This paper introduces model distillation learning (MDL), a novel approach that enables a custom network to learn from the black-box prediction of the target network using only their shared input-output data. Furthermore, this paper shows that the proposed approach achieves superior results in certain applications compared to alternative methods, and the successful development of a model distillation learning framework that learns from the data and parameters of the target network, which has significant implications for emerging applications like Internet of Things and cloud computing.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have set upper limits on the branching fractions for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ and $\bar{B}^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ with a 90% confidence level. The branching fraction of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ is less than 14.8\times10^{-6}. Additionally, upper limits have been placed on the branching fractions for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ (< 20.6\times10^{-6}), $\bar{B}^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ (< 16.7\times10^{-6}), and $B^0_s,\bar{B}^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0}\bar{K}^0$ (< 6.6\times10^{-6}), based on 3.8\,{\rm fb} of $pp$ collision data collected at 8\,{\rm TeV}.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducible elements, it's not clear which elements can be submodules of a given module. However, for modules that have no infinite descending chains, we can successfully apply order-embedding technique to demonstrate that Stanley's link-extension algorithm can be utilized to construct the entire lattice of submodules, including their join irreducible submodules. Furthermore, we can further build the lattice of submodules for certain direct sums of cyclic modules, including some modules over the integers. As an example, the process of constructing the lattice of submodules of a specific 2-generated $Z_{12}$ module over the integers using Stanley's algorithm is detailed.

A strong geodetic subset of a graph $G$ is a subset $S$ such that every vertex in $G$ can be linked to two distinct neighbors in $S$ through the shortest and unique path containing no other vertices from $S$. In this study, we determine the minimum cardinality of such subsets, known as the strong geodetic number, and explore its variants where the requirements are relaxed or intensified. Additionally, we calculate these numbers for specific graph constructions, including power of cycles and certain graph products.

The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can provide a large dataset easily. Although these paths aren't great solutions themselves, they still hold some value since they show the agent's movements in the task's environment, potentially containing useful information for imitation learning. This study investigates suboptimal and agnostic paths' efficiency in improving performance across three common skills that rely on learning from sound visual cues from a first-person perspective. We establish that suboptimal and agnostic paths can enhance imitation learning performance when other data sources are hard to come by, but they may hinder performance with vast quantities of optimal expert examples. This study also develops a straightforward, data-driven strategy for combining these paths with optimal expert data to maximize performance.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from one another, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios, of varying complexity, showcases the superiority of the co-sampling method over single expert demonstrations. The source code for the study is openly accessible at this link: https://github.com/zhenghuashan/Co-Imitation-Learning.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance, which is significantly better than the standard Hamming distance, for using sequence detection on polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. Our proposed function is proven to create a maximum likelihood decoding algorithm, and it is demonstrated that its excellent error-correction capabilities cannot be outperformed by any other coding method. A efficient coding technique is also proposed, and for a specific code and high data rates, it is proven that our method's complexity complexity complexity is comparable to low-density parity-check codes. Our findings are supported by simulation results for the proposed code and technique under Rayleigh fading conditions.

Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation pre-training can significantly improve neural machine translation. Nonetheless, this approach faces issues due to the massive action space size associated with the encoder's output. While sparse action techniques have achieved notable success, they've also introduced a critical drawback by forcing the use of a large vocabulary, thereby hindering effective RL training. Our research introduces a counterintuitive concept, suggesting that a smaller vocabulary size is advantageous for RL post maximum likelihood estimation pre-training. We've developed a method called the Rejected Sampling (RJ) to identify high-probability actions post pre-training. The RJ $\rho$-volume method was also introduced to further enhance RJ by targeting actions within a specific probability density range. Experimental results on standard benchmark datasets have confirmed that reducing the vocabulary size with RJ has produced improved outcomes over the original RL method.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that requires no pre-defined robot model and can be achieved through image analysis alone. This system, based on advanced image processing and optimization techniques, has been fully implemented in C++ and is currently being tested on real data. The system's flexibility and efficiency have been further enhanced by the development of a Python interface that allows for easy experimentation with different algorithms and processing steps. When applied to real-world data, the system produced accurate calibration results with minimal errors and a high degree of reliability.

This study introduces two key concepts, quasi-finitely separating maps and quasiapproximate identities, which form the basis for the definitions of QFS-spaces and quasicontinuous maps. Building upon these definitions, various properties and characteristics of QFS-spaces are investigated. Key findings include: Firstly, any QFS-space is inherently a quasicontinuous space; secondly, closed subspaces, as well as quasicontinuous projection spaces, derived from QFS-spaces are themselves QFS-spaces; thirdly, continuous retracts of QFS-spaces possess the same characteristic and specific types of QFS-space retracts can be constructed; lastly, upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces correspond to FS-spaces.

The rise of partisanship seems to be rising across various metrics including voter behavior and online engagement. Research into the Web's influence on polarization has produced several key findings in the past, but much remains unclear. We investigated online news consumption patterns and identified a new phenomenon - the online echo chamber effect, where individuals tend to consume content that aligns with their pre-existing views. We observed this effect specifically in the US market, where users display a strong preference for news aligning with their political ideology in their browsing habits. This tendency is even more pronounced among partisan users and influences both the type of content users engage with and the websites they visit. Our research also uncovered distinct online echo chamber effects operating within partisan groups on different website configurations. Echo chamber effects are part of a broader set of previously unidentified differences in online news consumption behavior that vary based on the political makeup of the population being studied. These effects highlight distinct patterns in online consumption that are unrelated to users' ideological alignments.

We examine the Lehnert and Schweitzer proof that the word problem for Thompson's group V has a non-context-free property. We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages, and for some of its generators, the combined cyclic variant of four deterministic context-free languages is sufficient. This relationship reveals that the time complexity of solving V's word problem deterministically is no more than quadratically scaling with input size.

The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly captivating 
because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine discrete time-driven
dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to its surroundings.
Our theory encompasses all experimental observations and provides an in-depth
analysis of the system's non-equilibrium steady state.
Our findings show that periodic driving forces and the characteristics of the 
environment can be precisely managed to ensure that there is continuous energy 
exchange between the open system and the surroundings, thereby making it possible to 
achieve any desired value of this current and characterize the resulting 
non-equilibrium steady state.

We explore how several established recurrent operators including curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators contribute substantially to biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal within the Euclidean space.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed examination to evaluate the impact of QCD axion mediators on the e+e- collider forecast and the impact of dark sector particles on the LHC's future capability to find neutrino oscillation parameters and axion-nucleon couplings, conditioned on dark matter's primary composition being axionic. The results include the possibility of n$\gamma$ and n$\gamma^*$ measurements in future n$\gamma$ colliders allowing for the neutrino mass ordering and the possibility of dark sector masses within the 5-50 MeV range being feasible in future e+e- colliders. The outcomes also include future LHC dark matter searches constraining dark gluon portal and electron sector masses, while dark sector gluon and electron masses influence dark matter auto-annihilation and ensure an adequate dark matter density. The model's various features and findings are illustrated through contour plots and the article concludes with a summary and discussion of the limitations and future directions of research.

Between October 2019 and February 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$-band plates simultaneously, testing the feasibility of this approach. A total of four spectra were collected for 200 target stars, with 119700 spectra picked for a follow-up survey with 200 spectra per plate. Although most spectra had a signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 in the LAMOST survey, some stars' spectra were over-exposed or missing parts of the spectral range due to the limited number of masks available. Ultimately, the study found that the LAMOST could successfully collect data from multiple $K$-band plates simultaneously, with the quality of the spectra comparable to those obtained from a single plate. Although there were some discrepancies in radial velocity measurements, the results showed that stars could be accurately classified using the LAMOST data. Additionally, the study indicated that the LAMOST survey could increase the number of collected objects by up to three times using multi-plate data.

In image recognition, particularly in medical Rader, the use of convolutional neural networks is highly effective. This is because edge features are vital in such applications and can be extracted through differential convolution operators akin to mathematical differentiation in mathematical analysis. This operator produces similar neural network responses to adjacent pixels or intensity changes, effectively mimicking the role of mathematical differentiation. This novel approach, which gives emphasis to such features, has resulted in improved performance in medical Rader experiments compared to the conventional approach using orthogonal normalization.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transaction protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to two-sided commits. To better understand how MongoDB provides transactional consistency across its various deployments, we focused on the atomicity aspect, as other properties such as isolation and durability are fairly standard in NoSQL databases. Depending on the deployment scenario, we found that the atomicity guarantee in MongoDB is mediated through either client-side or server-side mechanisms, respectively. Additionally, in the sharded cluster deployment, the size of the critical section can be significantly reduced through client-side two-sided commits, thus facilitating client-server network partition tolerance. In contrast, server-side two-sided commits result in a larger critical section. Ultimately, in the event of a detected crash, the protocol switches to an alternative approach to ensure data integrity.

Using the elementary symmetric function basis, we re-express the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths with a bounce number of three via a combinatorial interpretation related to the inverse of the Kostka matrix from Egecioglu-Remmel (1990). This analysis shows the positivity of specific coefficients and confirms $e$-positivity for an expanded class of these functions, beyond a particular instance explored in Cho-Huh (2019).

We begin by defining a task for few-shot continual learning and propose a theory to explain how executive function works through a self-updating decision-making system. This idea is applied to build a simple neural network model that can build on previous knowledge to master new skills quickly through a limited number of examples, or through a continuous learning process. The results of our study support our theory, as the proposed model's performance surpasses traditional passive learning models and knowledge-based executive function models in multiple benchmark tests across a range of standard datasets.

The success of medical image analysis using machine learning largely relies on high-quality datasets. However, the presence of biases in these images can significantly compromise the performance of these models. Although research has extensively addressed bias in natural image datasets, the problem of bias in medical imaging is less explored. In this study, we investigate the issue of bias in analysis models for X-ray images, specifically in bone age assessment from left elbow radiographs. Our investigation reveals that models can be susceptible to biases present in these images, leading to poor performance when encountering new data. Furthermore, we identify demographic-related features in these models, which raise ethical concerns. On the other hand, our team developed a framework to mitigate model vulnerability to image biases, which demonstrated superior results compared to existing methods. Ultimately, our work provides a crucial foundation for further exploration of bias in medical imaging and the design of safer machine learning models in this field.

Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social networks has gained momentum due to its potential to uncover fundamental patterns and relationships that are missing in simpler models. Geometric frustration in condensed matter physics has already provided significant insights and unexpected phenomena, such as strong quantum fluctuations in otherwise classical systems, extensively studied for decades on triangular lattices. However, the structure of these studies typically separates sites into magnetic and non-magnetic environments, obscuring the impact of frustration-induced quantum effects on a uniform lattice. This is where our work comes in; using an exact analytical approach, we explore a Heisenberg model on the Frushon lattice - a quantum graph where every node is interconnected with at least two others, enabling us to derive precise results for both classical and quantum regimes. Our findings highlight the robustness of our method against variations in lattice size and interaction strength, ultimately revealing the formation of magneto-elastic domains within the system.

We analyzed solar wind energy flux in close proximity to the Sun using data collected by the PSP spacecraft from November 2018 to June 2020. By comparing our measurements to those taken farther away from the Sun by the STEREO-A spacecraft, we aimed to quantify energy flux normalization at 1 solar radius. The results showed an average normalized solar wind energy flux of $1.06 \pm 0.04$ during intervals when the solar wind had been traveling for less than 15 days since its origin. We found no evidence of significant energy gain or loss as the solar wind approached Earth's orbit. We observed higher normalization values during solar events, suggesting possible imbalances between expanding solar tornadoes and contracting background sheath regions. The findings suggest that turbulence and the solar magnetic field contribute equally to the total magnetic energy flux within the solar wind.

Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of this technology often drops when it's applied in real-time situations. While adversarial training has shown great potential in improving speech processing tasks, its application to emotion recognition from speech requires further investigation. This research explores the feasibility of using adversarial training to enable a network to understand the emotions conveyed in audio recordings. Building on the generator-discriminator framework, our approach introduces the concept of an emotion judge and presents three distinct adversarial training models. These models employ both competitive and collaborative dynamics to develop the ability to recognize the emotion in speech and convey an emotional tone. We evaluate our proposed methods on two prominent data sets, finding substantial improvements in cross-domain and multi-domain scenarios, as well as the ability to inject emotion into monotone speech.

We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO) under high pressure effects on its structural, magnetic, electronic, and optical properties using first-principles calculations. Initially, we determined the lattice parameters and angles for its P6$_3$mc phase up to 30 GPa. Subsequently, we induced a phase transition to its para-magnetic state and found the band gap to remain stable before decreasing significantly. We also determined the effective masses of carriers in valence and conduction bands. Finally, we examined the band structure and density of states, discovering a shift in Fe 3$d$ states towards lower energies under pressure. A BFTO sample was also studied experimentally using a resistivity measurement in a high-pressure setup, which showed a sudden increase in resistivity at around 2.5 GPa at 5 K, 300 K, and 4.2 K, which was found to be attributable to a magnetic phase transition from ferromagnetic to paramagnetic state.

Hybrid methods tackling continuous shortest path problems start by local optimization
of discrete shortest paths in spatial networks. The convergence to optimal solutions
depends on the discretization error caused by restricting the global search to a network,
with specific implications on the choice of network density. A notable application
is flight planning, which involves determining optimal routes considering factors such
as flight time, fuel consumption, and weather conditions. Advanced algorithms for
discrete shortest paths can be used to compute starting points for locally convergent
methods in optimal control. We establish a priori and localized bounds for the
error in estimated flight times compared to optimal continuous trajectories, taking
into account network density and wind field. These bounds facilitate designing
networks with optimal connectivity, and the derived bounds are illustrated through
benchmarks, which show significant improvements in localization but still offer scope
for refinement through additional estimators.

Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both approximate analytical and exact numerical methods to solve self-similar equations. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the shape of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate is determined as a function of hadron recoil. This rate is reconstructed via the $D_s^{-}$ decay sequence into $K^-K^+\pi^-$, following $D_s^{*-}$ decay into $D_s^{-}\gamma$. The resulting rate is fit with CLN and BGL form factor parametrisations, yielding final results for both models.

A recent paper provides an analysis of advancements made in categorizing monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with rational potential properties. A specific subset of these solutions is composed of generalized Hermite polynomials, and it is demonstrated that their associated potentials allow for exact expressions for eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of a polynomially bounded, periodic operator on the real line. Furthermore, this study reveals that these generalized Hermite polynomials correspond to a specific type of Calogero-Moser system, and their construction is facilitated by the realization of these systems as multiple orthogonal polynomials, ultimately enabling the derivation of their monodromy-free conditions through differential-difference relations known as SOS decompositions.

A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we examined the complex dynamics of a flow system stimulated by a single-frequency forced vibration. We utilized a three-dimensional phase space to reconstruct attractors and determined their correlation dimensions through analysis, confirming the presence of chaos in lines exceeding the correlation dimension. We also established a relationship between the chaos's measure and the size of the correlation dimension, providing implications for using this system in testing measurement tools and testing methods for detecting chaos in signals.

In epitaxial InAs/Al structures, our experimental analysis reveals the stochastic behavior of planar Josephson junctions and SQUIDs as temperature varies, exhibiting a crossover between macroscopic quantum tunneling and phase diffusion. The threshold temperature for this phase transition, T*, can be manipulated by adjusting a gate. The observed switching probability distributions are in line with minimal capacitance and moderate resistance, causing the switching current to be only a small portion of the critical current. Furthermore, synchronization between two JJs can cause a disparity in the switching current when comparing measurements of a single JJ versus that same JJ within an asymmetrical SQUID loop, where T* can be fine-tuned through applied magnetic flux.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within thermal quantum field theory. By incorporating temperature effects and spatial compactification via Thermofield Dynamics, corrections to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are calculated for both zero and finite temperatures.

This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit solutions for simple payoff functions and demonstrates the applicability of its model through numerical examples, including the 2007 AIG event.

By applying variational techniques, we develop a limiting model for a set of functionals subject to two-scale periodic constraints, facilitating the study of energy storage within high-contrast composites with microstructures at nanoscale.

We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal characteristics of over 500 massive early-stage galaxies, utilizing data from the Subaru Telescope's TMT Legacy Survey. Our analysis revealed that the findings from this study are representative of the broader population of these galaxies due to sample size adequacy. We discovered an unusual observation wherein nearly half (specifically 44% with a margin of 7%) of the studied galaxies were associated with significant tidal structures exceeding 1% flux, in contrast to the预期值 of about 0.5%. This discrepancy highlights the potential for prominent tidal features around massive galaxies in the local universe, which has implications for understanding future observations from next-generation large telescopes. Additionally, we established an upper limit of 100 square arcminutes for the size of the TMT LS survey, which affects our current research but is anticipated to be significantly larger than previously estimated.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers avenues for exploring more intricate relationships between different socioeconomical groups in various societal settings.

The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in CPA and nonlinear optical research, and in turn, drives advancements in multiple fields, including medicine, data communications, and industrial sector. This review begins with an overview of CPA and NLO principles and their interconnection, followed by comprehensive examinations of specific CPA and NLO system configurations, including those utilizing a single pass, dual-pass setups, resonators, and optical parametric amplifiers. The paper's structure facilitates a comparison of various CPA and NLO system configurations, and ultimately, our goal is to provide CPA and NLO researchers with an up-to-date, easily accessible reference.

We maintain fixed $p \in [1,\infty)$ and $K \in (0,\infty)$ and a probability measure $\mu$. It is demonstrated that for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, there exist linear maps $\pi_n \colon \ell_p^n \to \ell_p^{k_n}$ with $k_n \le Cn^{1-2/p+\varepsilon_n}$ such that for any collection $\{f_1,\dots, f_{n+1}\} \subset \ell_p^n$ where the maximum value of $\mu(\{|f_i - f_j| \ge K\})$ among all $1 \le i < j \le n+1$ does not exceed $1/4$, the following inequality holds:
$$
\max_{1 \le i < j \le n+1} \mu(\{| \pi_n(f_i) - \pi_n(f_j)| \ge CK\}) \ge 1/4 - \varepsilon_n.
$$
This finding is complemented by an example showing that a different class of linear maps can increase the $\ell_p^{n+1}$ distortion by a factor of $n^{1-2/p+\varepsilon_n}$.

In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-crowded beams to provide crucial input for analysis. The emittance scans provided valuable insights into the longitudinal and transverse beam properties, bridging the gap between specialized tests and regular production runs. They offered in-depth insights into the interconnections between a beam's longitudinal and transverse properties. The significance of emittance scans will continue to grow with the increased dynamic range and novel closed-orbit bump techniques for beam separation that will be implemented at the LHC in 2017 through the upgrade to the final focusing triplet in beam pipe B at upgrade point B.

This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to significant energy waste, financial loss, and slowed convergence. In our research, we examine a generic multi-agent setup where the environment is deterministic and captures the characteristics of a large, distributed system with numerous identical agents. We then develop and evaluate two reinforcement learning algorithms through computer simulations, utilizing the ArviZ package for statistical analysis, in order to address optimization issues under attack. Our findings demonstrate that utilizing match-making to identify and exclude adversarial agents is more effective than simply discarding their input data, particularly when dealing with multiple malicious agents.

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that are vulnerable to various sources of atmospheric and instrumental noise. A significant challenge lies in achieving extremely sensitive experiments with sufficient signal-to-noise ratios. This paper introduces a novel approach for estimating regularized costs of functions of an experimental network's components, regardless of their functional form, and illustrates the method's effectiveness through its application to the regularization of radiative transfer equations in the context of cosmic microwave background experiments. This specific scenario is crucial for examples involving multiple layers of polarized films commonly used in these experiments. A key finding from our research indicates that even with the inclusion of temperature and polarization noise, the most complex regularized form reduces to the sum of two simpler cross-coupled scattering temperatures. This discovery has the potential to significantly influence the design of upcoming experiments planned for launch in 2021 and beyond.

In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods introduce minute alterations in images and videos, underscoring the importance of designing a detection method capable of leveraging both spatial and frequency domain information. To achieve this, we propose a novel network architecture, the Multi-Domain Frequency-aware Attention Network (MD-FAN), which extracts multi-domain features and refines attention across spatial and frequency domains. Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets, including FaceForeniscs, OC-Sales, and DeepFaceDiscovery6, demonstrate MD-FAN's accuracy, consistency, and robustness in distinguishing real from deepfake content, surpassing existing state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, we establish the validity of multi-domain analysis for deepfake detection and assess the efficacy of multiple synthesis methods, revealing that these approaches are less real-like than occlusion-based approaches.

This paper examines how LDPC codes perform in relation to their check node degrees over a binary erasure channel, specifically focusing on the BPEC performance under degree-degree correlations as described by a general degree-based message passing model. Our research identifies two key strategies to enhance finite-size BPEC performance: ensuring small-degree check nodes connect with small-degree variable nodes, and reducing check node degrees relative to their corresponding variable nodes. These optimal strategies align with those previously established for optimal degree distributions in the threshold saturation model. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical connection between the threshold behavior of the general message passing model and that of the LDPC ensembles that follow optimal degree distributions, providing insight into how they relate to each other.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach, called "quantum key distribution with device imperfections exploited", leverages the inherent defects in these systems to enhance their security and adaptivity. By allowing for frequent and unannounced switch-overs between various operating modes, our method prevents potential attackers from gaining a substantial advantage, thus reducing their information about the final shared key. We demonstrated this protocol's efficacy in simulations, showing that it can significantly improve the performance of the commercially available QKD system, called ID Quantique's "ID-2000", especially at high distances.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and optimizing strategies within the Multi-access Edge Computing paradigm. Our approach involves online algorithms for virtualized resource scaling, reconfiguring computing and communication assets, and enabling dynamic BS switching to minimize energy consumption and ensure Quality of Service (QoS). Numerical results demonstrate that these strategies lead to significant reductions in edge computing and communication costs, promoting energy efficiency and cost-effectiveness in MNs by minimizing unnecessary BS activations.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems.

Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$ over the rational numbers, with an embedding into the complex numbers that places conjugate elements in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$. Let $\mathcal{O}$ be a finite-dimensional structure of dimension $n$ within the complex numbers. The successively ordered minimum values $\gamma_i$ of the structure $\mathcal{O}$, when scaled by the square root of the discriminant of the number field, form a sequence $\mu_i = \frac{\sqrt{\mathrm{disc}(K)}}{\sqrt{8}}\,\gamma_i$ for elements $1 \leq i \leq n-1$. This work investigates whether certain bounded regions in the space of possible values for these sequence elements have a measurable area and perimeter, and determines if the area and perimeter are both equal to zero.

We utilize 1-d fs/ps hybrid rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy with dual probes to make comprehensive measurements of gas temperature and rotational temperature. By harnessing the power of time- and frequency-domain measurements, we achieve precise predictions of several gas properties, including the index of refraction, absorption coefficients, and line shapes, in real-time. The technique showcases remarkable sensitivity, sufficient to detect the weak dual-probe S1 signal and extract accurate temperature readings,同时 it also reveals the dependence of accurate predictions on accurate diagonal FSR calibration.

The traditional theory of planetary formation through core accretion has limitations when explaining how small particles overcome early development obstacles in a protoplanetary disk. A more recent model proposes the viscous ring-instability to account for ring structures in protoplanetary disks. It suggests that particles may reduce the disk's conductivity, inhibiting the growth of instability. Using GPU-based simulations of interacting gas and dust, this study investigates this model's validity. As the disk evolves, ring structures become unstable, breaking into smaller whirlpools, and subsequently forming stable dust formations. These structures provide ideal environments for the growth of planetary building blocks through gravitational collapse and the streaming instability. Observational data on exoplanets supports this process and creates favorable conditions for planetary system formation.

Quantum Hall phases exhibit gapped behavior in the interior while supporting both chiral and neutral edge modes.  A specific setup involving a path that only includes neutral modes, which experience a magnetic field, can generate a measurable current when a voltage is applied at one end and the other end is shorted.  It is proposed that the neutral mode's ability to carry information can be harnessed to recover the current that flows when only a voltage is applied at one end and the other end is open.  A similar approach can also reconstruct the recovery current in the one-end-open scenario.  Notably, this last case is chiral, making direct observation of the recovery current possible.  Finally, an experiment is described that uses a dc electroluminescent diode to demonstrate the presence of a surprising current in a specific direction when the magnitude of a specific recovery current exceeds the magnitude of another current, both with opposite directions.

We introduce a rigid cluster model to achieve a representation of the quantum group U_q(g) for Lie algebras of type ADE. This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the quantum group U_q(g) to a subalgebra within the quotient of Weyl group invariants from the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). Leveraging the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we find that U_q(g) possesses a natural basis \bar{Θ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Furthermore, the basis \bar{Θ} maintains an invariance property under the braid group action defined by Lusztig, Dynkin's automorphisms, and the star anti-involution.

In our research, we address the challenge of designing a communication-efficient and privacy-protecting method for training machine learning models across multiple devices. To tackle this issue, we introduce DR-DSGD, a robust decentralized optimization algorithm that training a model with Distributionally Robust Stochastic Gradient Descent (DR-RSGD). By utilizing the technique of gradient encoding, we enable DR-RSGD to resist various attacks, resulting in a more resilient training process. Unlike traditional DSGD, which can be compromised, we show that a robust learning approach can significantly reduce communication costs while still providing privacy protection. By leveraging the power of robust learning, we discover a way to train models more efficiently with less communication. To validate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we conduct several experiments, which demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD in achieving both efficient communication and privacy preservation.

We have developed and refined new methods to compute pressure estimates for hard-disk systems, suitable for implementation on GPUs. These techniques are built upon existing variance-reduction approaches but offer improvements in variance management that can handle multiple values of $N$ (number of particles) and $R$ (radius) simultaneously. We have tested our algorithms on systems with $N/ \pi R^2$ values ranging from $10^{-2}$ to $10^{2}$ and found that they produce highly accurate pressure estimates, verifying a phase-transition phenomenon in hard-disk systems that was initially described by different equations of state.

Jet modifications within a nuclear medium are influenced by jet nuclear interactions, such as jet quenching and nuclear absorption, as well as changes to the initial state of the system. To comprehensively understand jet nuclear interactions, it's essential to understand how jets traverse different types of media, such as those produced in heavy-ion collisions, proton–nucleus and nucleus–nucleus collisions at various energies and from different production angles. JEWEL+MC@NLL simulations of jet nuclear interactions in proton–nucleus collisions at LHC energies have demonstrated that p$p$-based jet baseline choices significantly impact the magnitude of jet nuclear interactions. To mitigate these P$\_$t-dependent biases, a new set of baseline jets has been introduced. Furthermore, the study indicates that jet nuclear interactions exhibit similar scaling behaviors with $p_T$ across different energy scales (e.g., $p$p$, $p$${p}$p$${p}$p$, and nucleus–nucleus collisions), and that cold matter effects on the incoming parton have a negligible impact on the magnitude of jet nuclear interactions.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions and connections within these schemes, researchers have turned to web traffic analysis for detection. Although some success has been achieved, some members of pyramids use multiple identities, known as mule accounts, which distort traffic statistics and render some detection methods ineffective. In this study, we formulate a new approach to studying these multinode connections in pyramidal structures and introduce a novel, mathematically based way to identify them. Our method also offers a means to estimate the global size of these schemes with remarkable accuracy - in one case, we found the scheme in question had nearly ten times the global user base that was initially thought.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. Due to dense crowding in the bulge region, discovering new candidates is challenging. Utilizing data from the VISTA Variable Velocity Vector experiment and Two Micron All-Sky Survey, particularly in the $I$ band, researchers identified 12 newly described globular cluster candidates in the Galactic bulge.
