When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved assessing the methods' performance under various noise levels.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete data set $\mathbf{y}$ and recover an image $\mathbf{u}$ that, when transformed through a known degradation process $ \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}(\mathbf{u}) + \mathbf{e}$, results in the observed $\mathbf{e}$ has zero-mean Gaussian noise. To achieve this, they draw samples from the posterior distribution $p(\mathbf{u}|\mathbf{y})$ and evaluate it using metrics like Negative Logarithmic Likelihood (NLL). Unfortunately, an extensive study by Jin et al. has shown that even after $M$ iterations, where $M$ can be significantly larger than the total number of pixels in $\mathbf{u}$, the NLL of sampled $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ still exceeds that of a simple Gaussian prior, making it impossible for $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ to outperform a basic solution. To investigate whether this failure persists with more rigorous evaluation metrics and for larger datasets, we conducted a comprehensive analysis using the Super-Resolution task, in combination with multiple evaluation methods, including the Structural Similarity (SSIM) index, Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), and a dataset consisting of $1024 \times 1024$ images. This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds.

Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that can only be achieved through terahertz communication. To optimize data transfer in this frequency range, smart reflecting surfaces can shape signal propagation. By incorporating energy harvesting into SWRS systems, we can design a reflection pattern that maximizes both data transfer and energy transfer simultaneously. To solve this complex problem, an iterative algorithm is proposed, which is then simplified using geometric analysis for easy implementation. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of both the algorithm and the simplified solution.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. We used wideband data from the RASA array to study a high latitude screen associated with pulsar J1939+2338. A custom interstellar scintillation analysis tool was employed to track the screen's varying intensity at different frequencies. The screen's size and orientation were determined from long baseline observations, along with its transverse speed, which was found to be 27.15 km/s and directed away from the Sun. The screen's column density and turbulence were also calculated, along with its radio brightness, which exceeds the surrounding interstellar medium. Notably, the screen's size and orientation may be similar to those containing hidden HII regions. These findings illustrate the value of pulsar interstellar scintillation in mapping and tracking individual scales of interstellar scintillation.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) that utilizes a pitch-dependent Dilated Convolution Neural Network (DCNN) to create steady-state harmonic signals, with applications in audio analysis, synthesis, and manipulation. In cases of non-stationary signals, such as speech or musical instruments, analyzing and synthesizing individual harmonics by quaternions allows for a breakdown of the fundamental frequency, amplitude, and phase (FAP) from the DCNN, facilitating a novel, FAP-conditioned harmonic synthesis (HARSYN) by leveraging the learned harmonic structures, resulting in superior reconstruction performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods. In voice synthesis, this method allows for high-quality harmonic signal reconstruction, leading to harmonic-stable Text-to-Audio (T2A) synthesis when combining with existing synthesis pipelines and FAP learning/estimation when FAP trajectories are automatically extracted or manually input, allowing for harmonic-controlled voice rendering with distinct harmonic characteristics, and even harmonic-dissociated synthesis when PQT masks and FAPs are independently generated, allowing for unexpected harmonic combinations, and resulting in improved harmonic reconstruction performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

This research presents a novel annotation and correction tool for Arabic texts,
namely MADARi, catering to Standard and Dialectal varieties. MADARi offers a user-
friendly interface and efficient management capabilities for annotated texts. Its
core features encompass a comprehensive set of morphological annotations, including
part-of-speech, gender, number, person, pronoun status, and lemmata for each word,
as well as a detailed dependency parse. Additionally, MADARi offers customized
interfaces for different Arabic varieties and an open-source, web-based platform for
collaborative annotation and collaboration among users.

Planets that are cool and located close to their host stars often have atmospheres 
that are chemically active and can undergo significant changes due to photochemical 
reactions. These reactions are significantly influenced by the presence of ammonia, 
especially in atmospheres that are rich in hydrogen. To understand this better, 
we performed a comprehensive set of numerical simulations and a detailed examination 
into the reactions of ammonia in the atmospheres of four planets that are owned by 
their host stars, using both self-consistent and non-equilibrium rate schemes. 
Our analysis revealed that the interaction between ammonia and methane results in the 
formation of a prominent hydrogen haze and the appearance of distinct chemical 
absorption in the visible and near-infrared spectra of these planets. 
Interestingly, our models also showed that ammonia can exist in its equilibrium form in 
the cooler interiors of these planets, which could potentially be observed using 
high-resolution spectroscopy and future direct imaging missions. 
However, in the warmer regions of these atmospheres, the intense heat causes 
ammonia to break down into its constituent components, significantly altering 
their chemical composition. 
Our research highlights the importance of ammonia in shaping the chemical 
processes that occur in the atmospheres of temperate planets that are rich in hydrogen, 
which in turn has implications for their spectral appearance and the development of 
their atmospheric models.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperatures decrease in proportion to T^(2r-1), with r defined as the exponential product of the resistance and a universal constant divided by the Planck's constant, non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks will not display this specific temperature dependence. Furthermore, tunneling conductance for states other than those at zero energy will also exhibit different changes when the lead's resistance is increased, resulting from both peaks associated with a quantum critical point and ghost peaks resulting from the scattering of an electron between states with opposite charges by the voltage drop across the high-resistance lead. These inner-peaks can be merged to achieve a form of "series normalization" that effectively reduces the conductance to that of a single-electron orbit, thereby restoring the peak heights for states other than those at zero energy to their original values, while the height of the Majorana peak is reduced by the increase in resistance.

The development of advanced detection algorithms through deep learning has accelerated the identification of road issues, including automatic defect detection and marking analysis. To expedite and reduce costs associated with manual inspections, a comprehensive system called RoadAtlas has been developed, providing a holistic solution encompassing road flaw detection, marking parsing, interactive data visualization through a web interface, and a robust database framework supported by API tools.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving equivalence under Morita inversion. Through the use of double categories and orientation bicategories, this paper explores the invariance properties of shadows, demonstrating that they too exhibit Morita invariance, an earlier proven concept by Schlichting for topological Hochschild homology (THH).

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically identifies challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Notably, our method's design allows for easy deployment on smaller models, resulting in a 4.1x reduction in computational capacity while maintaining competitive accuracy.

Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have significantly boosted their effectiveness in natural language processing, social network analysis, and biomedical data interpretation, particularly in scale-free and hierarchical graphs. While Euclidean geometry-based techniques have achieved notable success, recent studies suggest that hyperbolic geometry may offer even more efficient representations for such graphs. Although current work has successfully integrated GNNs into the hyperbolic framework, most approaches employ a single type of hyperbolic geometry, ignoring the varied intrinsic curvatures present in real-world graphs. This study proposes G^2, a flexible GNN framework capable of utilizing diverse curvatures in hyperbolic geometry, both theoretically and practically. By designing an original algorithm to optimize the average curvatures of the graph and its subgraphs, G^2 enables a more precise representation of real-world graphs. Experimental evaluations across five datasets demonstrate the superiority of G^2 over state-of-the-art methods, particularly in node classification and graph drawing tasks.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate.

A new method has been created that successfully transfers squeezed states into optical cavities even in stable conditions. The method builds upon conventional optomechanical setups, utilizing a three-level atom to facilitate the transfer. Two techniques were devised to observe the squeezed state transfer effect, including applying a controlled influx of squeezed phonons and simulating the system in an environment of phonon-squeezed vibrations. Our model demonstrates the ability to efficiently achieve this transfer in optomechanical systems.

We examine an expansion of modal $\mu$-calculus, specifically considering its application to sets comprised of fundamental elements and investigate its core properties. Our analysis reveals that model checking for this variant of the calculus is undecidable when applied to general structures, however, it becomes feasible when evaluated on bipolar graphs. Furthermore, our study shows that the set of basic elements for modal $\nu$-calculus is non-computable on basic structures, although it is decidable when the structure in question is cyclic. We also explore a limiting case of the expanded calculus and prove that it allows for efficient model checking. This result is significant as it enables the resolution of the basic problem in a computable manner when the given structure is not bipartite.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom, while other options result in incorrect theories.

A signed graph is created by adding a polarity to the edges of an existing graph, and this concept of signed graphs has recently been integrated with other graph theory ideas like minors and coloring. By examining the notion of extended $N_0$-precoloring expansions, this work explores the relationships between graph minors and coloring, and it proves that certain expansions are realizable for any given graph and precoloring, specifically showing that they remain invariant under the equivalence of Conder's star operations.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transformation, exposing the complex symplectic matrix that dictates the entire thermal equilibrium state and thereby determines its thermal properties. Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics, each embodying a distinct category of thermalization dynamics including parabolic and elliptic dynamics, hyperbolic dynamics, and most general loxodromic dynamics, with a particular emphasis placed on thermal equilibrium states for ultrastable systems, commonly found in thermodynamics and statistical mechanics, characterized by focus points with hyperbolic or loxodromic dynamics, featuring unique quadratic thermal potentials comprising four components: time, space, space-time, and inverse space, with a particular attention given to harmonic oscillators and their dynamics, showing that both elliptic and hyperbolic dynamics belong to a broader category of quadratic Hamiltonians.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. This new insight is crucial for the fields of statistical mechanics and thermodynamics. Negative temperature arises from an inverse relationship, where the system's energy increases as temperature decreases below this threshold. It is crucial to note that systems with negative temperature are not hotter than those with positive temperature; in fact, they appear colder. This apparent paradox can be explained by considering that negative temperature represents an extremely high energy state, akin to a deeply frozen system. This concept is further illustrated through the discussion of population inversion and its association with negative temperature. A simple and tangible model, such as the two-level system, is used to clarify the counterintuitive properties of negative absolute temperature.

Let G be an abelian group and A a nonempty subset of G, with elements indexed as $a_0, a_1,..., a_{k-1}$. For any positive integer h less than or equal to k, we can calculate a restricted signed sumset denoted as $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$, which comprises sums of $a_i$ with weights from {-1,0,1}. The goal of this article is to solve the minimum value of $|h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A|$, where $|A|$, when A is a set of integers, and investigate the underlying structure of A to achieve this minimum value. Additionally, some open questions related to $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$ are proposed in this article.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9000 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 360 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for developing and testing novel multilabel multiclass classification methods. We've evaluated several state-of-the-art multilabel multiclass classification methods, focusing on models that can be trained with a limited number of samples per class, with the goal of facilitating real-world clinical deployment. Our initial findings suggest characterizing datasets divided by genotype may enhance the performance of such models.

A novel numerical approach has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues with plane wave illumination, especially effective in handling high-frequency scenarios. This method's framework can also apply to time-dependent problems and other types of incident waves. The algorithm combines the hybrid high-order method for interior domain discretization with an asymptotic approximation using the parabolic cylinder function for boundary evaluation, reducing the problem's complexity to a manageable form. Through rigorous convergence analysis and testing with time-dependent wave problems, the method's accuracy and reliability have been confirmed with quantitative error estimates showing second-order accuracy under specific conditions.

We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three ocean finds in Ivju (1986), Macalini 36.1 (1986), and Shergotty 36.2 (1986). Our research discovered that the water content in these pyroxene minerals ranged from 15 to $295$ parts per million, with δD values varying between $-105$ and $+289$ per mil. The water content and δD values found in pyroxene from Benenitra and Chelyabinsk were similar to those found in ordinary chondrites with thermally altered histories, indicating a potential link to the source of water in the parent asteroid and a possible preservation of primordial solar system volatiles during the differentiation process. Benenitra, however, stands out as a distinct case, with distinctly different δD values compared to other ordinary chondrites altered to degree D3 or higher, which suggests that the degree of alteration in its parent asteroid was D2 to D3 and that pyroxene from ocean finds with similar degrees of alteration also exhibits δD values consistent with those found in Benenitra.

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find exact expressions for scalar products and form factors of higher-spin XXZ chains. This applies to any spin values and mixtures thereof. We verify the affine quantum-group symmetry, $U_q(\hat{sl_2})$, for the XXZ chain's monodromy matrix, enabling exact derivation. Specifically, we use quantum-group symmetry to explicitly obtain diagonalized forms for the B and C operators within the F-basis of the spin-1/2 XXZ chain. This achievement substantiates prior conjectures about the algebraic Bethe-ansatz's correlation function calculations. These results provide a crucial foundation for systematic studies of the XXZ chain's physical and mathematical properties.

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches offer improved results but are extremely resource-intensive. To overcome these challenges, we explore two two-stream network architectures for zero-shot translation, enabling the conversion between any pair of languages from among the source and target languages without additional training. These architectures utilize both speech-to-text and text-to-text translation translations and leverage the capabilities of speech recognition, including utilizing textual data from source and target languages and the capacity to perform audio-to-text conversion. Building on this multi-task learning framework, we introduce and experiment with two proposed models: an additive model that sums the transformed speech and text inputs before decoding, and a cross-modality attention model that integrates the speech and text modalities during decoding. Our method enhances zero-shot multilingual translation by reducing the need for repeated translation and leveraging the high-quality multimodal input. Notably, our two proposed two-stream models achieve zero-shot multilingual translation with at least a 2.45 improvement in the sum of the BLEU scores across all target languages from a single source language in the zero-shot translation tasks.

We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime.

This study introduces two categories of elements in the algebra U(gl(n)), specifically double Young-Capelli bitableaux and central Schur elements, both exhibiting central or irreducible properties respectively. The definition of the central Schur elements is rooted in a double Young-Capelli tableau construction, utilizing two Young-Capelli tableaux of complementary complementary Schur shape. Notably, this definition has been shown to be equivalent to Ogden's 2015 formulation. A key consequence of these results is the establishment of primary decomposability for the irreducible U(gl(n)) modules, with their highest weight links to specific Schur elements. Furthermore, a formula for the Jantzen filtration of these modules is also derived.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at the minimum dark sector integration scale, whereas the "solar" scale arises as a radiative correction. We determine the parameter ranges for dark matter that allow for a coherent explanation of the neutrino and dark matter characteristics, including a potential solution to the LHC muon $g-2$ anomaly.

We employ our recent global fitting approach to previously reported global structure and bonding minimum energy data, derived from extended X-ray absorption fine structure measurements, to reevaluate the $e_g/t_{2g}$ orbital state ratios in various transition metal oxides. Even for well-studied compounds, like TiO$_2$ and TiO, significant variations in local bonding environments can cause $e_g/t_{2g}$ ratios to be masked, producing deceptive interpretations of spatially averaged experimental data, as TiO$_2$ and TiO serve as prime examples. However, our method enables global bond length data to be utilized globally, yielding good predictions for previously unexplained UNR cases, like TiSe$_2$ and TiSi$_2$, where local bond lengths were found to be perfectly described with no need for occupied core state potential adjustments.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain birational transformations known as Floppings. Specifically, we investigate the Flop transformation for toric complete intersections and explain its impact on relative Minkowski scalars and quantum orbifold cohomology. Additionally, we propose a quantum Birch Swinnerton-Denny map and show its preservation of quantum CH 0 cycle values.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Although GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from CycleGAN, we achieved high fidelity in translating healthy X-rays into ones showing various pathology signs. Furthermore, we examined the model's capacity to detect and reproduce specific organ级 changes resulting from different encoded pathologies. Our research also utilized radiologists' input to evaluate the accuracy of the generated alterations. Our findings indicated that the model can effectively simulate certain pathology effects, including those arising from medical procedures and producing organ-level changes. By leveraging the research's included datasets, researchers can examine the model's ability to create various types of pathology. Our results also showed that the model performed better in creating organ-level changes compared to patient-level changes.

ViDaExpert is an application for exploring and researching multidimensional vector information using various techniques, including histogram of vectors, SVVD, and multidimensional spectral analysis. Built on top of the MultiDAStan statistical framework and ViDa visualization tools, ViDaExpert enables rapid assessment of data relevance and identifies significant frequency ranges through interactive multidimensional spectral analysis. By integrating the force-directed multivariate method (FDMM), the program can also handle and visualize complex multidimensional data sets, facilitating further investigation of real-world applications such as speech signals, radar data, and financial time series. An user-friendly web interface for the MultidDA web service allows seamless access to AI-driven multidimensional analysis from any web-connected device.

Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex-shaped regions is crucial in various applications, where the domains often have intricate boundaries. When the function defining the interior of such a complex shape is unknown, numerical methods like Monte Carlo or quasi-Monte Carlo are commonly used. These methods require an parameterization of the boundary to compute line integrals. We propose utilizing Green's third identity to evaluate the potential, which eliminates the need for such a parameterization. This approach becomes particularly advantageous for quasi-Monte Carlo methods, methods based on sparse grids, or tensor products of 1D rules. We demonstrate the performance of our method for such a product-based approach and discuss cases where it outperforms conventional methods.
